title: Backwards planning / Begin with the end
desc: Planning from the intended curriculum outcome or performance and working backwards to the prerequisite knowledge, intermediate steps, practice and assessment evidence.
text:
What it is: Planning from the intended curriculum outcome or performance and working backwards to the prerequisite knowledge, intermediate steps, practice and assessment evidence.
Why it helps: A clear endpoint improves alignment: explanations, tasks and checks are selected because they build the required knowledge rather than because they are convenient or engaging in isolation.
Use it when: planning a unit, a lesson sequence or any high-leverage task whose success depends on several knowledge steps.
Implementation sequence
Specify the precise end performance and the knowledge students must retrieve or apply.
Break the endpoint into prerequisite and component steps; identify the likely bottleneck.
Sequence examples and practice from secure foundations towards greater complexity.
Plan what evidence will show readiness to move between steps.
Review whether every activity and resource serves the endpoint.
DO | DON'T
 Write an exemplar or success description before planning the route. Keep the endpoint ambitious and common while planning routes into it. Build retrieval and cumulative practice into the sequence. |  Plan a string of activities before defining what students will learn. Confuse task completion with mastery of the intended knowledge. Treat the plan as fixed when checks show a prerequisite gap.
Check for impact
Students can explain how each task connects to the intended outcome.
Later practice draws on knowledge deliberately secured earlier.
Sources informing this profile: BSCS Teaching and Learning Policy; StepFinder: Lesson Preparation and Optimise Communication.

title: Plan the explanation
desc: Deliberately scripting the conceptual route, key language, examples, representations, misconceptions and stopping points before teaching new content.
text:
What it is: Deliberately scripting the conceptual route, key language, examples, representations, misconceptions and stopping points before teaching new content.
Why it helps: Planning reduces avoidable ambiguity and frees the teacher to monitor attention and understanding during delivery. It also helps separate essential detail from interesting but distracting information.
Use it when: new or difficult content, explanations involving diagrams or demonstrations, and points where previous classes have developed predictable misconceptions.
Implementation sequence
Name the one idea students must understand by the end of the explanation.
Activate the minimum relevant prior knowledge and define unfamiliar vocabulary.
Chunk the explanation into coherent steps with one purpose per step.
Select examples, near-miss non-examples and representations that reveal the concept.
Script precise phrases, likely questions and checks for listening and understanding.
Rehearse aloud and remove any detail that does not serve the goal.
DO | DON'T
 Plan where to pause, point, reveal and check. Use consistent terminology and sentence structures. Prepare an alternative representation for the likely sticking point. |  Rely on slides to do the explaining. Introduce several new ideas before checking the first. Add extra facts that increase load without increasing understanding.
Check for impact
Students can restate the key idea using the intended vocabulary.
Checks reveal understanding of the concept, not merely recall of the teacher's words.
Sources informing this profile: BSCS Policy Appendix 1; StepFinder; DistilED: Explaining with Precision and Science of Simplicity.

title: Plan the means of participation / Double plan
desc: Planning both teacher actions and the cognitive actions students will take: thinking, retrieving, writing, discussing, explaining and revising.
text:
What it is: Planning both teacher actions and the cognitive actions students will take: thinking, retrieving, writing, discussing, explaining and revising.
Why it helps: Teacher activity can conceal student passivity. A participation plan distributes opportunities to think and makes the intended learning behaviour observable without mistaking compliance for learning.
Use it when: any explanation, questioning sequence, discussion or feedback episode in which only a small number of students might otherwise respond.
Implementation sequence
For each lesson phase, write what students will think about and how they will respond.
Choose the response mode to match the knowledge: individual writing, whole-class response, paired rehearsal or individual explanation.
Front-load the means of participation before asking the question.
Plan movement from Everyone to Together to Anyone, retaining individual accountability.
Identify students who may need pre-call, writing time, vocabulary or an adjusted access route.
DO | DON'T
 Protect private thinking time before public response. Use whole-class methods to sample everyone at pivotal points. Plan follow-up prompts that deepen rather than merely repeat answers. |  Write only what the teacher will say or show. Use hands-up as the default sampling method. Add paired talk without deciding what students should produce afterwards.
Check for impact
Across a lesson, every student repeatedly says, writes or does something connected to the content.
The teacher can explain why each participation method was selected.
Sources informing this profile: BSCS Policy; StepFinder; DistilED: Everyone, Together, Anyone; Tips for Teachers: Cold Call and Turn and Talk.

title: Plan the exemplar and plan the error
desc: Preparing a high-quality model response and the misconceptions, weak examples or incorrect processes most likely to occur.
text:
What it is: Preparing a high-quality model response and the misconceptions, weak examples or incorrect processes most likely to occur.
Why it helps: An exemplar clarifies the destination; planned errors help the teacher diagnose thinking and design explanations or distractors that address causes rather than symptoms.
Use it when: high-leverage questions, extended responses, complex procedures and tasks with recurring misconceptions.
Implementation sequence
Complete the task yourself in the form students are expected to produce.
Annotate the essential success features, vocabulary, decisions and presentation.
List likely errors and classify them as knowledge, attention, process, fluency or self-regulation gaps.
Create a near-miss response or distractor for each important misconception.
Plan how students will compare, diagnose and improve examples before revising their own work.
DO | DON'T
 Select only the features students can realistically apply next. Use contrasting examples to make quality and misconception boundaries visible. Keep the final correct record available after analysis. |  Present a polished model without revealing how it was produced. Use obviously absurd wrong answers that reveal nothing about thinking. Ask students to improve work without time or a precise action.
Check for impact
Students can identify and reproduce the essential success features.
The teacher's planned distractors correspond to actual response patterns.
Sources informing this profile: BSCS Policy Appendix 1; StepFinder: Exemplar Planning, Plan for Likely Errors and Hinge Questions.

title: Annotated seating plans and purposeful adult deployment
desc: Using current knowledge of pupils to position students and adults deliberately, annotate practical supports, plan talk partners and define circulation or check routes.
text:
What it is: Using current knowledge of pupils to position students and adults deliberately, annotate practical supports, plan talk partners and define circulation or check routes.
Why it helps: Seating and adult roles influence attention, participation, visibility and independence. Proactive planning reduces reactive intervention while avoiding dependency on a teaching assistant.
Use it when: every class, particularly where attendance, talk partners, sensory needs, literacy barriers or adult support materially affect access.
Implementation sequence
Maintain an up-to-date plan that matches the actual room layout.
Annotate concise, strategy-focused information rather than sensitive detail or labels alone.
Plan purposeful pairs, temporary triads and adjustments for absence.
Mark teacher and, where relevant, teaching-assistant circulation and check routes.
Brief additional adults on the learning goal, vocabulary, misconceptions, prompts and feedback to gather.
Review the plan when needs, relationships or response evidence change.
DO | DON'T
 Use annotations such as 'pre-warn before cold call' or 'check written instruction understood'. Keep the teacher connected to pupils with SEND and lower prior attainment. Use adults to promote independence through prompts, clues and models. |  Group students routinely by label or perceived ability. Make the teaching assistant the default teacher for pupils with SEND. Leave sensitive annotations visible to pupils or visitors.
Check for impact
All pupils have a viable talk partner and access to teacher attention.
Support results in greater independence rather than permanent adult dependence.
Sources informing this profile: BSCS Policy: Seating Plans and Appendix 5; StepFinder: Seating Plan and Classroom Layout strategies.

title: Solid entry routines and threshold
desc: A short, explicitly taught sequence for moving from corridor to classroom and beginning independent learning immediately.
text:
What it is: A short, explicitly taught sequence for moving from corridor to classroom and beginning independent learning immediately.
Why it helps: Predictability removes logistical uncertainty, protects learning time and secures attention before working memory is occupied by avoidable transitions.
Use it when: the start of every lesson and whenever entry has become slow, noisy or dependent on repeated teacher reminders.
Implementation sequence
Prime students at the threshold and greet them with calm warmth.
State a small number of observable entry expectations.
Control the flow, direct students to assigned seats and make the Do Now immediately accessible.
Scan, use non-verbal cues and positively narrate successful entry.
Rehearse or reset the routine when the standard is missed.
DO | DON'T
 Keep materials and starter location consistent. Build brief positive interactions without interrupting the routine. Use Do It Again proportionately to secure the standard. |  Begin giving academic instructions while students are still entering. Change the entry procedure from lesson to lesson. Use a whole-class reset when a quiet individual correction would suffice.
Check for impact
Students begin the Do Now without prompting and within the expected time.
Teacher attention is available for relationships and diagnosis rather than logistics.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Solid Entry Routines; StepFinder: Establish an Entry Routine; BSCS Policy: Threshold and Do Now.

title: Signal for attention and habits of attention
desc: A consistent cue followed by observable, inclusive attention behaviours that prepare students to listen, look or think about the intended content.
text:
What it is: A consistent cue followed by observable, inclusive attention behaviours that prepare students to listen, look or think about the intended content.
Why it helps: Attention is the gateway to learning. A rehearsed signal reduces transition time and ambiguity, while habits such as empty hands, orienting to the speaker and active listening protect cognitive bandwidth.
Use it when: before explanations, instructions, peer contributions, demonstrations and any transition from activity to shared attention.
Implementation sequence
Select one calm auditory or visual signal and explain its purpose.
Define what students should do when the signal occurs using observable directions.
Model, rehearse and time the routine until it becomes fluent.
Signal, pause, scan the full room and use least-intrusive corrections.
Begin only when the agreed standard is met; adapt the form for legitimate sensory or neurological needs.
DO | DON'T
 Use the same signal consistently across lessons. Separate securing attention from checking that instructions were understood. Praise rapid, complete transitions with precise narration. |  Repeat or raise the volume of instructions over partial attention. Treat eye contact as the only valid sign of attention. Use a theatrical cue that is harder to sustain than the routine itself.
Check for impact
The class moves to the agreed attention posture quickly and without repeated prompts.
Students can recall and act on the instruction given immediately after the signal.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Signal for Attention, Habits of Attention and Securing Attention; Tips for Teachers: Checks for Listening.

title: Routines, transitions and precorrections
desc: Teaching repeated classroom processes explicitly and priming students immediately before predictable difficulty points.
text:
What it is: Teaching repeated classroom processes explicitly and priming students immediately before predictable difficulty points.
Why it helps: Routines reduce decision load and maximise learning time. Precorrections make the desired behaviour salient before the moment, preventing rather than merely reacting to predictable errors.
Use it when: movement, equipment, pair talk, practical work, book distribution, transitions and any routine with repeated friction.
Implementation sequence
Script the routine as a short sequence of observable actions.
Explain the purpose, model it and check behavioural understanding.
Rehearse in chunks, then practise the complete sequence with a visible time limit.
Before a high-risk moment, prime the likely error and the desired alternative.
Scan, narrate success and reset only the part that needs more practice.
DO | DON'T
 Use concise cues that become shared classroom language. Assign roles for complex transitions. Review routines after holidays or when membership changes. |  Assume students know the routine because it was explained once. Correct after the transition without teaching what should replace the error. Overload the routine with too many verbal steps.
Check for impact
Transitions become faster and require fewer teacher prompts.
The predictable error decreases after a specific precorrection.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Classroom Transitions and Precorrections; StepFinder: Establish Routines.

title: Positive narration, precise praise and motivation
desc: Reinforcing the actions, effort, quality and norms that support learning while building belonging, competence and value.
text:
What it is: Reinforcing the actions, effort, quality and norms that support learning while building belonging, competence and value.
Why it helps: Students are more likely to invest attention when success feels attainable and the task feels worthwhile. Describing effective behaviour also gives peers a concrete model without interrupting learning.
Use it when: after directions, during independent practice, at moments of persistence and when establishing a new classroom norm.
Implementation sequence
Position and scan deliberately for the behaviour or work quality you want to reinforce.
Name the observable action and, where useful, connect it to learning.
Use non-verbal acknowledgement for low-key reinforcement.
Narrate effort, revision and successful strategy use rather than fixed traits.
Follow up important work so students see that it has value.
DO | DON'T
 Keep praise authentic, specific and proportionate. Engineer early success before asking for greater persistence. Build relationships outside correction moments. |  Use generic praise that gives no information about what worked. Praise speed when accuracy or reasoning matters more. Use public praise in a way that embarrasses an individual.
Check for impact
Students repeat the reinforced behaviour without escalating rewards.
Participation and persistence broaden beyond the initially confident pupils.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder: Motivate Students to Learn and Reinforce Positive Behaviours; DistilED: TCMH.

title: Least-intrusive correction and behavioural leadership
desc: A calm graduated response that starts with visibility, proximity or non-verbal cues and escalates only as needed while preserving dignity and learning time.
text:
What it is: A calm graduated response that starts with visibility, proximity or non-verbal cues and escalates only as needed while preserving dignity and learning time.
Why it helps: Low-intrusion responses prevent secondary conflict and keep attention on learning. Clear, predictable consequences and take-up time reduce debate and emotional escalation.
Use it when: low-level off-task behaviour, talking, lateness, refusal or argument that must be addressed without derailing instruction.
Implementation sequence
Position for visibility and use deliberate scanning.
Try proximity, eye contact, a gesture, self-interrupt or positive narration nearby.
If needed, describe the behaviour and direct the required action briefly.
Use private correction, partial agreement or a directed choice where appropriate.
Allow take-up time, then check compliance and apply the agreed sanction consistently.
Follow up and rebuild the relationship after the lesson.
DO | DON'T
 Separate the primary behaviour from secondary reactions. Use a calm, firm tone and economy of language. Follow the school behaviour system consistently. |  Enter a public debate about fairness during instruction. Stack several corrections without allowing take-up time. Ignore serious or unsafe behaviour in the name of low intrusion.
Check for impact
Corrections become shorter and students return to learning quickly.
Repeated incidents reduce because follow-up and routines are consistent.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Behavioural Leadership Map, Behaviour Management Ten Tools and TCMH; StepFinder: Respond to Negative Behaviours.

title: Making participation safe
desc: Designing predictable, high-success participation in which students can think, speak, practise and make mistakes without humiliation while expectations remain ambitious.
text:
What it is: Designing predictable, high-success participation in which students can think, speak, practise and make mistakes without humiliation while expectations remain ambitious.
Why it helps: Anxiety and social risk consume attention. Predictable routines, preparation time and warm responses reduce that cost so students are more willing to expose their thinking and learn from error.
Use it when: cold call, public sharing, show call, pair talk and classes where silence reflects fear rather than lack of ideas.
Implementation sequence
Explain the purpose and routine for participation before using it.
Provide private thinking, writing or paired rehearsal before higher-risk responses.
Use warm invitations, pre-call and sentence stems where needed.
Normalise errors and respond to them as useful information.
Address ridicule or dismissive reactions immediately.
Keep the intellectual standard high while adjusting the route into participation.
DO | DON'T
 Make the process predictable and the content demanding. Praise bravery, revision and improved second attempts. Use frequent low-stakes participation so no single response feels exceptional. |  Use surprise or public exposure as a motivational device. Lower the challenge to avoid the possibility of error. Allow confident students to dominate because they volunteer.
Check for impact
A wider range of students attempts answers and revises them publicly.
Errors produce analysis rather than laughter, silence or withdrawal.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Making Participation Safe; Tips for Teachers: Cold Call, Call and Respond and Turn and Talk.

title: Everyone, Together, Anyone (ETA) and active participation
desc: A participation framework that moves between responses from everyone, structured thinking with a partner and individual accountability.
text:
What it is: A participation framework that moves between responses from everyone, structured thinking with a partner and individual accountability.
Why it helps: Different modes reveal different evidence. Whole-class responses create universal commitment, paired talk rehearses and refines ideas, and individual questioning probes reasoning while keeping everyone prepared.
Use it when: planning a sequence of checks, explanations or discussion in which participation would otherwise be left to chance.
Implementation sequence
Identify the thinking required: recall, application, explanation, evaluation or revision.
Use Everyone methods such as mini-whiteboards, writing or choral response for universal commitment.
Use Together methods for rehearsal, comparison and elaboration.
Use Anyone methods such as cold call to sample and probe individual reasoning.
Respond to the evidence and vary the mode rather than repeating it mechanically.
DO | DON'T
 Front-load how students will respond. Preserve an individual product before collaboration. Use the sequence flexibly rather than treating it as a fixed three-step formula. |  Assume visible busyness means students are thinking about the content. Use paired talk as a break from teacher talk without a question worth discussing. Collect responses without adapting instruction.
Check for impact
Every student produces repeated visible or audible evidence of thinking.
The teacher's sampling becomes more representative of the class.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Everyone, Together, Anyone and Active Participation; BSCS Policy: Participation and Thinking Ratio.

title: Cold calling
desc: Asking the question to the whole class, allowing thinking time and then warmly inviting a selected student to respond.
text:
What it is: Asking the question to the whole class, allowing thinking time and then warmly inviting a selected student to respond.
Why it helps: Pause-then-name keeps every student accountable for thinking and produces a more representative sample than relying on volunteers. Frequent, supportive use reduces stigma and builds a culture of contribution.
Use it when: across lesson phases for recall, explanation, comparison, listening checks and sampling longer written responses.
Implementation sequence
Explain that cold call is an invitation and a way to include everyone, not to catch students out.
Secure attention, ask the question to all and give at least several seconds or appropriate writing time.
Scan thinking, then select strategically or randomly according to the purpose of the check.
Invite the response warmly; support volume and precision.
Probe, sequence several answers or return after paired/written rehearsal.
DO | DON'T
 Use question-pause-name rather than name-question. Mix direct cold call with pre-call, paired rehearsal and written preparation. Use indicator students when their response would reveal an important gap. |  Use cold call only for behaviour management or when someone is inattentive. Select a student before giving the rest of the class a reason to think. Abandon the student after 'I don't know' without a second chance.
Check for impact
More students prepare answers even when they are not ultimately called.
Responses become fuller and participation is distributed more equitably.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Cold Calling and Equitable Questioning; Tips for Teachers: Cold Call.

title: Wait time
desc: A deliberate pause after a question and a second pause after a student's response before the teacher evaluates or moves on.
text:
What it is: A deliberate pause after a question and a second pause after a student's response before the teacher evaluates or moves on.
Why it helps: Thinking, retrieval and formulation take time. A pause increases the number of students able to prepare and improves the likelihood of reasoned rather than impulsive responses.
Use it when: questions requiring explanation, inference, calculation, recall from longer-term memory or use of precise vocabulary.
Implementation sequence
Explain why silence will follow questions and normalise it as thinking time.
Ask the question before choosing a respondent.
Pause for roughly 3-5 seconds or longer where complexity demands it.
Maintain neutral scanning without signalling the eventual respondent.
After the answer, pause again so the speaker can extend and peers can process.
DO | DON'T
 Display complex questions so transient wording remains available. Use writing when the cognitive demand exceeds what can be held mentally. Combine wait time with cold call and follow-up questions. |  Fill the pause by rephrasing, hinting or answering your own question. Apply the same fixed pause to every question regardless of complexity. Interpret a fast confident response as proof of understanding.
Check for impact
More students can offer a prepared answer when sampled.
Answers contain more reasoning, evidence and subject vocabulary.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Wait Time; Tips for Teachers: Check for Understanding and Cold Call.

title: Call and response / Choral response
desc: A clearly cued routine in which the whole class gives the same concise response in unison.
text:
What it is: A clearly cued routine in which the whole class gives the same concise response in unison.
Why it helps: It multiplies opportunities to retrieve and rehearse, supports pronunciation and fluency, and establishes collective participation. Its reliability depends on a single clear answer and disciplined cueing.
Use it when: short factual recall, definitions, formulae, pronunciation, technical vocabulary, routines and key statements students need to remember accurately.
Implementation sequence
Teach the cue and model the expected timing, volume and unison response.
Explain or ask the prompt, then allow thinking time before the cue.
Use a consistent signal such as 'Together in 3, 2, 1'.
Listen for participation and accuracy; repeat to improve precision where necessary.
Follow with individual or written checks when independent understanding matters.
DO | DON'T
 Use Explain-Frame-Reframe to check both directions of an important relationship. Cold call first, then bring the accurate response together chorally. Push for clear volume and full participation without shaming. |  Use choral response for open questions with several defensible answers. Assume a loud unison answer proves every student understands. Cue so quickly that students merely echo rather than retrieve.
Check for impact
All students can later produce the knowledge independently.
Technical vocabulary is pronounced and used accurately.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Choral Response; Tips for Teachers: Call and Respond.

title: Turn and Talk / Think-Pair-Share / Oracy
desc: Structured talk that begins with individual thinking, uses a focused paired exchange and ends with accountable sharing, writing or rechecking.
text:
What it is: Structured talk that begins with individual thinking, uses a focused paired exchange and ends with accountable sharing, writing or rechecking.
Why it helps: Exploratory talk helps students retrieve, organise, test and refine ideas. Rehearsal lowers the risk of public response, while explicit listening routines prevent domination and off-task talk.
Use it when: questions requiring explanation, comparison, justification or evaluation, especially when roughly 40-80% of the class has enough knowledge to help one another.
Implementation sequence
Give silent thinking or writing time before talk.
State the question, desired product, time limit and who speaks first.
Use prompts such as disagree and convince, add evidence, or explain why another answer differs.
Circulate without hovering; note strong ideas and misconceptions.
End on the crest of the wave, then cold call, compare responses or require summary writing.
Recheck with a related but different question when talk was used responsively.
DO | DON'T
 Make the pair the unit of accountability and praise effective collaboration. Test listening by asking students to report or evaluate their partner's idea. Use stable pairs and rehearsed switch/return cues. |  Use talk when fewer than about 40% have enough secure knowledge to contribute. Let discussion continue until energy and focus fade. Accept one partner dominating while the other remains unprepared.
Check for impact
Both partners can explain the shared conclusion and their reasoning.
A fresh check improves after discussion rather than merely sounding fluent.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Oracy for Learning and Think-Pair-Share; Tips for Teachers: Turn and Talk.

title: Second Chance / No Opt Out
desc: Returning to a student who could not initially answer after giving them time and access to peer responses, so that they still complete an intellectually meaningful response.
text:
What it is: Returning to a student who could not initially answer after giving them time and access to peer responses, so that they still complete an intellectually meaningful response.
Why it helps: A predictable return maintains accountability without humiliation and turns 'I don't know' into attentive listening, rehearsal and a successful second attempt.
Use it when: cold call, checks for listening and any questioning routine where students may genuinely be unsure or temporarily unable to formulate.
Implementation sequence
Acknowledge uncertainty neutrally and state that you will return.
Ask one or two peers for answers while keeping the original student listening.
Return and require the student to repeat, paraphrase, select, evaluate or add to an answer.
Praise persistence and the improved response, not merely compliance.
Follow up privately if repeated non-preparation reflects a routine or access problem.
DO | DON'T
 Keep the tone warm and the return predictable. Choose a second-chance task the student can complete meaningfully. Use peer answers as models, not as a public rescue. |  Forget to return after saying you will. Turn the exchange into a prolonged public struggle. Accept passive repetition when the student could explain or evaluate.
Check for impact
Students listen to peers because they may be asked to use the response.
The frequency of unprepared 'I don't know' responses decreases.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Second Chance; StepFinder/TLAC: No Opt Out.

title: Process questions and equitable follow-up
desc: Questions that probe how or why an answer was produced, ask for evidence, comparison or connection, and refine responses for precision.
text:
What it is: Questions that probe how or why an answer was produced, ask for evidence, comparison or connection, and refine responses for precision.
Why it helps: Correctness alone can hide insecure reasoning. Process questions make the method visible, strengthen metacognition and allow the teacher to diagnose the exact point of breakdown.
Use it when: after correct and incorrect answers, during modelling, and whenever transfer depends on understanding the underlying principle.
Implementation sequence
Model the kind of reasoning and vocabulary you expect to hear.
Ask a focused answer question, pause and listen without immediate evaluation.
Follow with how, why, evidence, first-step or comparison prompts.
Ask students to re-articulate with greater precision or in their own words.
Fade sentence stems while retaining the expectation to explain.
DO | DON'T
 Sequence from recall to explanation and application. Ask several students to answer or reformulate the same high-value question. Use elaboration stems temporarily for pupils who need a route into academic speech. |  Accept the first correct answer and move on automatically. Round up a partial answer by completing the reasoning yourself. Use follow-ups so broad that students cannot identify the required thinking.
Check for impact
Students can name the principle or step that justifies an answer.
Misconceptions become locatable rather than appearing as unexplained wrong answers.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Process Questions, Elaboration Sentence Stems and Equitable Questioning; StepFinder: Add Challenge or Scaffolds Whilst Questioning.

title: Mini-whiteboards for participation
desc: A routine in which every student commits a short written, symbolic or multiple-choice response and reveals it on a common cue.
text:
What it is: A routine in which every student commits a short written, symbolic or multiple-choice response and reveals it on a common cue.
Why it helps: Simultaneous response raises participation, lowers the permanence of error and gives every learner a reason to think. It also prepares students for later explanation and discussion.
Use it when: short answers, calculations, diagrams, vocabulary, multiple-choice reasoning and book-to-board transfer during independent practice.
Implementation sequence
Teach equipment, silence, no-doodling, writing and reveal routines explicitly.
Standardise the expected response so boards can be scanned reliably.
Give at least 30 seconds or suitable think time before the show cue.
Use both sides or staged reveals to preserve independence and flow.
Select responses for cold call, comparison or whole-class discussion.
DO | DON'T
 Use concise prompts and consistent 'show me' cues. Scan priority students and every part of the room. Use book-to-board to make final answers visible during practice. |  Use boards for long extended responses better suited to books. Allow copying by letting answers appear at different times without control. Collect data and move on without feedback or adaptation.
Check for impact
Every student commits an answer before seeing peers' responses.
Participation remains high and routines consume little lesson time.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Mini-Whiteboards; Tips for Teachers: Mini Whiteboards.

title: Everybody Writes and accountable discussion
desc: Using brief individual writing before or after talk so every student develops, records and revises an idea.
text:
What it is: Using brief individual writing before or after talk so every student develops, records and revises an idea.
Why it helps: Writing slows thought, preserves an independent response and gives less confident speakers something to contribute. Post-discussion revision converts talk into a durable learning product.
Use it when: open questions, text analysis, comparison of methods, debate and feedback on student responses.
Implementation sequence
Set a tightly specified writing prompt and short time limit.
Circulate to identify ideas and select students for discussion.
Use paired or whole-class discussion to compare, challenge and refine.
Require students to revise, summarise or improve the original writing.
Sample the final product to check whether discussion moved thinking forward.
DO | DON'T
 Front the writing before discussion when independent thinking matters. Make the final written product explicit. Use displayed responses to compare quality and reasoning. |  Treat copying notes as evidence of thought. Let discussion replace an individual record of learning. Ask for lengthy writing when a short commitment would suffice.
Check for impact
All students have a response that becomes more accurate or developed.
Discussion draws on visible ideas rather than improvisation by a few.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder/TLAC: Everybody Writes, Front the Writing and Building Ratio Through Discussion.

title: Checking for understanding / TAPPLE
desc: A continuous feedback loop in which teachers ask, pause, select a response method, listen or look, interpret the evidence and act.
text:
What it is: A continuous feedback loop in which teachers ask, pause, select a response method, listen or look, interpret the evidence and act.
Why it helps: Learning is invisible unless elicited. High-quality checks replace unreliable perceptions with evidence and make teaching responsive rather than plan-driven.
Use it when: before teaching prerequisites, after each small input, at a lesson hinge and before independent practice.
Implementation sequence
Identify the newest or most important knowledge and likely misconception.
Ask a diagnostic prompt without leaking the answer through hints.
Pause long enough for everyone to think.
Pick an all-student response method where feasible; otherwise sample indicator students.
Interpret the pattern and decide whether to continue, clarify, model, practise or extend.
Recheck after the response so the loop is closed.
DO | DON'T
 Ask 'What have you understood about...?' rather than 'Have you understood?'. Use critique, error analysis, recall and explanation questions. Make any pre-check hint avoidable or delay it until after commitment. |  Use 'Any questions?' as the primary check. Treat volunteers, compliance or completed work as a representative sample. Collect answers without changing the next instructional decision.
Check for impact
The teacher can state what evidence prompted the adaptation.
A fresh question confirms that the identified misconception has reduced.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: TAPPLE and Check for Student Understanding; Tips for Teachers: Check for Understanding.

title: Hinge questions
desc: A pre-planned diagnostic question at a critical point where the class response determines whether teaching moves on, consolidates or reteaches.
text:
What it is: A pre-planned diagnostic question at a critical point where the class response determines whether teaching moves on, consolidates or reteaches.
Why it helps: Plausible distractors reveal specific misconceptions, providing more useful information than a simple right/wrong check and allowing a rapid whole-class decision.
Use it when: after a key concept, before a dependent step and before students move into independent practice.
Implementation sequence
Identify the precise concept on which later learning depends.
Write a clear stem and one defensible correct answer.
Create plausible distractors, each linked to a known misconception.
Collect simultaneous independent responses within a short time.
Ask students to explain choices where needed, then make the planned instructional decision.
Use a related follow-up to verify the response.
DO | DON'T
 Keep options balanced in length and free from accidental clues. Plan in advance what each response pattern will trigger. Use ABCD cards, fingers or whiteboards so everyone commits. |  Use trivial recall that does not genuinely affect the lesson route. Include joke or obviously implausible distractors. Discuss so long that the question ceases to be an efficient hinge.
Check for impact
Each distractor corresponds to an interpretable misconception.
The next teaching move follows the response pattern, not the original timetable.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Hinge Questions; StepFinder: Create Hinge Questions.

title: Mini-whiteboards for diagnosis
desc: Using standardised, simultaneous board responses to gather valid whole-class data quickly enough to adapt in the moment.
text:
What it is: Using standardised, simultaneous board responses to gather valid whole-class data quickly enough to adapt in the moment.
Why it helps: The teacher sees every response rather than extrapolating from a few voices. Controlled reveal and systematic scanning preserve independence and improve the validity of the sample.
Use it when: high-value short responses, calculations, diagrams, misconceptions, vocabulary and harder post-teach checks.
Implementation sequence
Plan the question, correct response and likely error patterns before teaching.
State the required format and give independent thinking/writing time.
Cue a simultaneous reveal; stagger only in a controlled way that prevents copying.
Scan systematically, including indicator students and the full field.
Give precise feedback and require correction.
Choose a responsive action and test it with a fresh board question.
DO | DON'T
 Use a question-mark convention for genuine uncertainty. Keep boards visible long enough to scan but not to invite answer changing. Ask students to lower boards before explanation so attention returns. |  Ask questions too broad to interpret at a glance. Focus only on the first few boards or the most confident students. Reveal the correct answer before students commit.
Check for impact
Response data is independent, simultaneous and interpretable.
Rechecks show whether the chosen adaptation worked.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Mini-Whiteboards; Tips for Teachers: Mini Whiteboards and Responsive Teaching.

title: Responsive thresholds and high success
desc: Using approximate success bands to choose a proportionate response while keeping practice in a productive zone, commonly around 80% success.
text:
What it is: Using approximate success bands to choose a proportionate response while keeping practice in a productive zone, commonly around 80% success.
Why it helps: High success supports motivation and reduces error practice, but perfection can indicate insufficient challenge. Thresholds turn response data into a practical decision rule rather than a vague impression.
Use it when: after a whole-class check, guided practice or a Do Now item when the teacher must decide whether to move on, use peers or reteach.
Implementation sequence
At roughly 80% or more correct, state or model the answer efficiently, move on and follow up the small group later.
At roughly 40-80% correct, use structured peer explanation or comparison, then recheck with a related but different question.
Below roughly 40% correct, provide a concise teacher explanation or model because there is too little secure knowledge in the room for peer teaching.
If performance remains weak after a response, track the gap and plan further teaching rather than endlessly extending the current activity.
Increase challenge gradually when success is consistently above about 90%.
DO | DON'T
 Treat the percentages as decision aids rather than rigid laws. Prepare follow-up questions and example-problem pairs in advance. Keep correction immediate and supportive. |  Probe or explain at length when nearly everyone is already correct. Use peer discussion when the room lacks sufficient correct knowledge. Move on below the threshold without a clear repair and recheck.
Check for impact
The response is proportionate to the actual class pattern.
A fresh check, not confidence or noise level, confirms improvement.
Sources informing this profile: Tips for Teachers: Responsive Teaching and Turn and Talk; DistilED: Obtain a High Success Rate.

title: Responsive micro-decisions
desc: A disciplined noticing-interpreting-responding cycle that asks whether understanding is secure, where the gap lies, whether to stay or pivot, whose thinking is missing and whether the response landed.
text:
What it is: A disciplined noticing-interpreting-responding cycle that asks whether understanding is secure, where the gap lies, whether to stay or pivot, whose thinking is missing and whether the response landed.
Why it helps: Classroom decisions are easily distorted by confidence, speed or the most visible students. Explicit decision questions keep attention on evidence and the underlying cause of error.
Use it when: during questioning, modelling and circulation when the planned route no longer matches what students are showing.
Implementation sequence
Probe before moving on: ask for the reasoning behind an apparently correct response.
Locate the cause: knowledge, process, explanation, fluency or self-regulation.
Compare expected and actual evidence; pause or pivot when they diverge.
Seek missing voices and evidence from indicator students.
After any response, ask a fresh question to test whether it landed.
DO | DON'T
 Name the diagnostic question you are answering before giving feedback. Use concise adaptations targeted at the identified cause. Record recurring patterns that need later curriculum attention. |  Give feedback before understanding the problem it is meant to solve. Continue an explanation solely because it was planned. Assume reteaching worked without re-sampling.
Check for impact
Adaptations become smaller, faster and better targeted.
The same misconception is less likely to persist unnoticed.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Micro-Decisions; BSCS Check and Adapt framework.

title: Adaptive teaching: high challenge, responsive support
desc: Maintaining a shared ambitious goal while adjusting explanation, representation, scaffolding, grouping, time or practice in response to barriers and live evidence.
text:
What it is: Maintaining a shared ambitious goal while adjusting explanation, representation, scaffolding, grouping, time or practice in response to barriers and live evidence.
Why it helps: Adaptive teaching avoids fixed ceilings and individualised parallel curricula. Proactive planning and micro-adaptations help more students access the same core learning.
Use it when: when vocabulary, prior knowledge, executive function, sensory access or response evidence shows that the current route is not working for some or many students.
Implementation sequence
Clarify the common learning goal and what will not be lowered.
Anticipate barriers and prepare models, visuals, prompts, vocabulary and alternative explanations.
Check everyone frequently and look for patterns rather than isolated slips.
Make the smallest useful adaptation: rephrase, model, scaffold, regroup, slow down or add guided practice.
Fade support and recheck progress towards the shared standard.
DO | DON'T
 Teach to the top while planning a way in. Use flexible groupings tied to the current barrier, not a permanent label. Prompt thinking before directly supplying answers. |  Create easier endpoints that cap attainment. Use the same scaffold for all students regardless of evidence. Let support become permanent or dependency-producing.
Check for impact
More students reach the common success criteria with decreasing support.
Groupings and scaffolds change as the evidence changes.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Adaptive Teaching; BSCS Policy: universal provision and anticipated barriers.

title: Checks for listening
desc: Brief, planned prompts that require students to reproduce, reframe or act on what has just been said, showing whether attention became usable information.
text:
What it is: Brief, planned prompts that require students to reproduce, reframe or act on what has just been said, showing whether attention became usable information.
Why it helps: Quiet appearance is a poor proxy for listening. A low-stakes check makes attention accountable and allows the teacher to repair missed instructions or key explanation points immediately.
Use it when: after instructions, definitions, a peer contribution or a key sentence in an explanation.
Implementation sequence
Plan the sentence, instruction or relationship that students must retain.
Warn the class that listening will be checked and secure full attention.
Use prompts such as 'Where will we answer?', 'What is step one?' or 'What did X say?'.
Use Explain-Frame-Reframe with cold call or choral response.
Correct least-intrusively, insist on 100% and repeat the instruction only when necessary.
DO | DON'T
 Use narrated countdowns and observable attention directions. Pause then name when cold calling the check. Check both the forward and reverse relationship in important statements. |  Assume silence means the instruction was processed. Ask only 'Are we clear?' or 'Does everyone understand?'. Repeat every instruction automatically, training students not to listen first time.
Check for impact
Students can accurately state or enact the instruction without peer copying.
Lost time from repeated explanations and instructions reduces.
Sources informing this profile: Tips for Teachers: Checks for Listening; BSCS Policy: Active Listening and Signal for Attention.

title: Do Now: retrieval-rich lesson start
desc: A short, immediately accessible and independently completed start-of-lesson routine, usually built around spaced retrieval rather than new content.
text:
What it is: A short, immediately accessible and independently completed start-of-lesson routine, usually built around spaced retrieval rather than new content.
Why it helps: The routine creates a purposeful start and uses retrieval to strengthen future access to previously taught knowledge. An achievable sequence also builds early success and gives the teacher useful response data.
Use it when: the start of lessons, with a separate prerequisite check later if new learning depends on particular knowledge.
Implementation sequence
Display about four clear, single-answer questions plus an optional challenge in a consistent place.
Sequence from an accessible first item to a more challenging final item, aiming for roughly three out of four correct.
Use a visible timer: approximately five minutes to complete and five minutes to review.
Circulate twice: first for routine and participation, then for response patterns and misconceptions.
Review responsively using one-question-at-a-time checks, book-to-board whiteboards, cold call or choral response.
Let latecomers join the current task and release one question at a time if focus is weak.
DO | DON'T
 Use spaced content from previous lessons and topics. Prepare concise models and follow-up items for likely errors. Move quickly when most students are correct and follow up the few later. |  Use the Do Now mainly to test prerequisites for today's lesson. Use ambiguous, trick or multiple-answer prompts. Allow review to become a lengthy reteaching episode.
Check for impact
Students begin independently with minimal teacher direction.
Retrieval accuracy improves across later spaced appearances.
Sources informing this profile: Tips for Teachers: Do Now; DistilED: The Do Now Checklist and Retrieval Practice.

title: Retrieval practice: spacing, challenge and feedback
desc: Effortfully recalling previously taught knowledge after some forgetting, with low stakes and feedback that makes the retrieval event itself part of learning.
text:
What it is: Effortfully recalling previously taught knowledge after some forgetting, with low stakes and feedback that makes the retrieval event itself part of learning.
Why it helps: Retrieval strengthens future retrievability. Spacing and appropriate difficulty create desirable challenge, while feedback prevents repeated recall of an error.
Use it when: Do Nows, quizzes, end-of-lesson review, homework follow-up and cumulative practice across a curriculum.
Implementation sequence
Map key knowledge across increasing intervals rather than relying on recent content.
Mix accessible and challenging items so students experience effort without routine failure.
Require recall before notes or cues are made available.
Provide an accurate answer and brief corrective explanation.
Schedule another retrieval opportunity, especially for weak items.
DO | DON'T
 Teach students how to self-quiz and mark accurately. Connect each item to curriculum knowledge rather than trivia. Keep stakes low enough that error remains informative. |  Use massed repetition or cramming as the main retrieval plan. Make every quiz a graded performance event. Assume a correct immediate answer means durable learning.
Check for impact
Knowledge remains accessible after longer intervals and in varied contexts.
Students can identify and revisit specific retrieval gaps.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Retrieval Practice - Seven Essential Principles; StepFinder: Ensure Consolidation and Retrieval.

title: Activating prior knowledge
desc: Bringing the specific existing knowledge needed for new learning into working memory and making the connection explicit.
text:
What it is: Bringing the specific existing knowledge needed for new learning into working memory and making the connection explicit.
Why it helps: New learning is understood by attaching it to existing schema. Activation reduces load, exposes missing prerequisites and makes meaningful rather than superficial connections.
Use it when: before a new concept, representation or procedure that depends on previously taught ideas.
Implementation sequence
Identify the smallest set of prior knowledge that genuinely supports the new idea.
Retrieve it through a brief question, example, diagram or comparison.
State the connection explicitly, moving from broad context to the precise link.
Ask students to process the relationship by explaining, predicting or comparing.
Check meaning rather than merely whether the old fact was recalled.
DO | DON'T
 Use a prerequisite check separately from spaced Do Now retrieval when needed. Supply missing background knowledge before building on it. Return to the connection during the explanation. |  Activate interesting but irrelevant associations. Ask only 'Who remembers...?' and rely on volunteers. Assume prior teaching means prior knowledge is currently accessible.
Check for impact
Students can state how the new idea builds on or differs from previous learning.
Misconceptions caused by missing prerequisites reduce.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Activating Prior Knowledge; BSCS Explain phase.

title: Small steps and precise explanation
desc: Breaking complex content into coherent, cumulative units and explaining each with concise, accurate language before immediate guided practice.
text:
What it is: Breaking complex content into coherent, cumulative units and explaining each with concise, accurate language before immediate guided practice.
Why it helps: Working memory is limited, especially for novices. Small steps reduce interacting elements and create repeated chances to check and correct before complexity accumulates.
Use it when: procedures, dense concepts, new vocabulary and tasks where one missed step prevents later success.
Implementation sequence
Define one micro-goal and link it to secure prior knowledge.
Explain and model the first step, including why it works.
Give every student an immediate attempt and check the response.
Correct or reteach before adding the next step.
Combine steps gradually and fade prompts once the sequence is secure.
DO | DON'T
 Use consistent terminology and repeated structures. Anticipate the misconception at each step. Move on when roughly 80% are secure, then follow up the few. |  Fragment content so much that the overall structure disappears. Add several dependent steps without a check. Confuse brisk pace with rapid teacher speech.
Check for impact
Students succeed on a similar item immediately after each modelled step.
They can explain the reason for the step, not just imitate it.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Small Steps and Explaining with Precision; StepFinder: Give Clear and Memorable Explanations.

title: Cognitive simplicity in slides and resources
desc: Designing explanations and materials so attention is directed to essential information: removing clutter, keeping related information together and retaining key transient information.
text:
What it is: Designing explanations and materials so attention is directed to essential information: removing clutter, keeping related information together and retaining key transient information.
Why it helps: Irrelevant detail, split attention and fleeting information consume limited working memory. Coherent design leaves more capacity for understanding and schema construction.
Use it when: slides, handouts, diagrams, worked examples and any explanation combining spoken and visual information.
Implementation sequence
Identify the message each slide or resource must carry.
Remove decorative images, duplicate text and unnecessary formatting.
Cue key information with consistent numbering, arrows, bold or highlighting.
Place labels and explanatory text beside the relevant visual.
Reveal in stages or dim completed material while keeping essential reference information visible.
Segment long material into familiar, predictable sections.
DO | DON'T
 Use meaningful visuals that directly support the spoken explanation. Pause speech while students read important text or labels. Use the school's accessible slide conventions consistently. |  Read dense text aloud while students are reading it. Use visual decoration that competes for attention. Separate a diagram from the explanation students need to interpret it.
Check for impact
Students look at the intended feature at the intended moment.
Fewer clarification questions arise from resource layout or transience.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Design Choices and The Science of Simplicity; BSCS Policy: PowerPoint Resources.

title: Worked examples and providing models
desc: Showing a complete or partially completed solution or product, with the structure, sequence and decisions made explicit before students perform independently.
text:
What it is: Showing a complete or partially completed solution or product, with the structure, sequence and decisions made explicit before students perform independently.
Why it helps: Novices can focus on the schema of the task rather than using working memory for unguided search. Multiple and faded examples create a bridge from observation to performance.
Use it when: multi-step procedures, extended writing, practical methods, diagrams and unfamiliar task formats.
Implementation sequence
Diagnose prerequisites and define the success criteria.
Present a complete example and reveal why each step or feature is present.
Ask students to identify, explain or compare key decisions.
Guide a similar example step by step, eliciting contributions from everyone.
Use completion problems or backward fading before independent application.
Return to the model when errors reveal an insecure step.
DO | DON'T
 Model at normal speed, then repeat slowly in chunks. Use strong, weak and near-miss examples for comparison. Keep the task stable while reducing support. |  Display a finished model without making the process visible. Ask novices to discover the method through trial and error. Jump directly from full model to a substantially different independent task.
Check for impact
Students can name and reproduce the process on a similar task.
Support can be removed without a collapse in accuracy.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Worked Examples and Provide Models; StepFinder: Use Modelling as a Scaffold.

title: Thinking aloud
desc: Verbalising the expert's internal decisions, monitoring and self-correction while completing a task.
text:
What it is: Verbalising the expert's internal decisions, monitoring and self-correction while completing a task.
Why it helps: Expert thinking is often invisible and automated. Narration reveals how to plan, select a strategy, notice difficulty, check progress and evaluate the result.
Use it when: tasks involving judgement, problem solving, reading comprehension, writing choices or strategic use of procedures.
Implementation sequence
Clarify the task and identify the decision points students cannot see.
Model a concise internal dialogue using first-person language.
Name the cue, relevant knowledge, option considered and reason for the choice.
Include a deliberate check or correction rather than presenting effortless expertise.
Invite students to explain the next decision, then practise their own think-aloud.
Fade the external narration into prompts for independent self-questioning.
DO | DON'T
 Script key decision sentences in advance. Separate narration of thinking from description of physical actions. Use subject-specific language accurately. |  Narrate every obvious action and overload the model. Present expertise as instant intuition with no monitoring. Let students watch passively without a subsequent attempt.
Check for impact
Students can articulate why they selected a step or strategy.
Independent work shows more self-checking and fewer avoidable process errors.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Modelling Through Thinking Aloud; StepFinder: Think Aloud and Model Metacognitive Strategies.

title: Examples, non-examples and variation
desc: Choosing positive examples, near-miss non-examples and deliberately varied cases to reveal the defining features and boundaries of a concept.
text:
What it is: Choosing positive examples, near-miss non-examples and deliberately varied cases to reveal the defining features and boundaries of a concept.
Why it helps: Examples alone can lead to over- or under-generalisation. Carefully controlled contrast focuses attention on the critical feature and supports transfer beyond a memorised surface form.
Use it when: concept formation, vocabulary, classification, quality criteria and misconceptions caused by superficial similarities.
Implementation sequence
Name the critical feature students must notice.
Choose a clear example and a near-miss non-example differing mainly on that feature.
Compare them side by side and ask what changed.
Use minimally different examples to isolate the feature, then maximally different examples to broaden the category.
Ask students to classify and justify new cases.
DO | DON'T
 Keep irrelevant features constant during the first contrast. Ask for the reason a case belongs or does not belong. Include common misconceptions as purposeful non-examples. |  Use absurd non-examples with too many differences. Explain only what is wrong without clarifying the boundary. Show a single prototypical example and assume transfer.
Check for impact
Students classify unfamiliar cases using the defining feature.
Overgeneralisation and undergeneralisation decrease.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Non-Examples; StepFinder: Explain for Deeper Understanding.

title: Visualiser, live drawing and dual coding
desc: Constructing writing, annotation, diagrams or models live while directing attention and revealing the decisions behind the representation.
text:
What it is: Constructing writing, annotation, diagrams or models live while directing attention and revealing the decisions behind the representation.
Why it helps: Live construction integrates words and visuals, reduces split attention and allows students to see a process unfold. Replication and explanation turn watching into active learning.
Use it when: annotation, diagrams, worked solutions, extended writing and improvement of student work.
Implementation sequence
Prepare the sequence, labels and likely difficult elements in advance.
Begin with a blank page and construct one meaningful element at a time.
Explain or think aloud, then pause speech while students read or copy labels.
Point or trace to direct attention and link new elements to prior knowledge.
Ask students to predict, replicate and explain the next part.
Close the loop with independent reproduction or improvement.
DO | DON'T
 Keep visuals functional and simple. Check sight lines and projection before teaching. Use the visualiser for student examples as well as teacher models. |  Create an over-detailed artistic diagram that hides the idea. Talk continuously while students are copying. Treat live display as sufficient without student practice.
Check for impact
Students can reproduce and explain the representation independently.
Their attention follows the intended part of the model.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: The Visualiser Guide and Live Drawing; BSCS Explain phase.

title: Storytelling, analogies and memorable explanation
desc: Using a concise narrative, analogy or metaphor to organise causal relationships and make an abstract idea easier to understand and remember.
text:
What it is: Using a concise narrative, analogy or metaphor to organise causal relationships and make an abstract idea easier to understand and remember.
Why it helps: A coherent narrative can build schema and direct attention through causality, conflict, complication and character. Its value depends on repeated connection to the concept rather than entertainment alone.
Use it when: content with causal sequences, human decisions, competing mechanisms or an abstract relationship that benefits from a familiar structure.
Implementation sequence
Work backwards from the one message or relationship students must retain.
Choose a narrative structure and a single clear thread.
Script concrete details, vocabulary and cause-and-effect links.
Use delivery, gesture and pauses to signal the key moments.
Return explicitly to the academic concept and test the mapping.
State where the analogy stops working to prevent misconception.
DO | DON'T
 Keep the story concise and purposeful. Repeat the key concept at several points. Ask students to explain the connection, not merely retell the story. |  Include entertaining detail unrelated to the learning goal. Use an analogy with important misleading features left unqualified. Let students remember the story while missing the disciplinary idea.
Check for impact
Students use the narrative to explain the causal or conceptual structure.
They can identify both the useful mapping and its limit.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Storytelling Checklist; StepFinder: Use Analogies, Stories and Examples.

title: Explicit vocabulary instruction with active practice
desc: Teaching a word's meaning, pronunciation, form, examples, non-examples and connections, followed by repeated retrieval and use in context.
text:
What it is: Teaching a word's meaning, pronunciation, form, examples, non-examples and connections, followed by repeated retrieval and use in context.
Why it helps: Vocabulary is both knowledge and a tool for thinking. Multiple encounters and active production make words retrievable and reduce language as a barrier to curriculum access.
Use it when: high-utility academic language, subject-specific terms and words whose everyday meaning differs from their disciplinary meaning.
Implementation sequence
Select a manageable number of essential words and prepare student-friendly definitions.
Model pronunciation and morphology; use choral rehearsal where appropriate.
Show the word in examples, non-examples and a meaningful visual or sentence.
Require students to use it through writing, paired talk and cold call.
Check for misconceptions and compare or connect related words.
Revisit through exit tickets and spaced retrieval.
DO | DON'T
 Keep definitions precise and consistent across resources. Provide sentence stems while students first use the word. Correct pronunciation and meaning immediately but supportively. |  Give a long word list without planned use. Rely on copying definitions as the learning event. Treat one correct use as secure long-term knowledge.
Check for impact
Students use the word accurately in new contexts.
Later retrieval is fluent without the original scaffold.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder: Teach New Vocabulary with Active Practice; DistilED: Choral Response and Non-Examples.

title: Guided practice
desc: Short supported rehearsal in which the teacher and students co-work examples, make responses visible and correct errors before independent release.
text:
What it is: Short supported rehearsal in which the teacher and students co-work examples, make responses visible and correct errors before independent release.
Why it helps: Guided practice bridges explanation and independence. Immediate feedback prevents misconceptions from hardening and builds the high success needed for confident practice.
Use it when: immediately after modelling each small step and before students attempt the complete task independently.
Implementation sequence
Frame the task as rehearsal and focus on one taught step.
Model the first item, then elicit the next steps from all students.
Use mini-whiteboards, cold call, pair explanation or completion problems.
Circulate and correct misconceptions immediately.
Fade prompts as accuracy improves and check for roughly 80% success.
Release to a closely matched independent task.
DO | DON'T
 Keep practice short, cumulative and visibly checked. Ask students to explain why the step works. Repeat a stage when response evidence is insecure. |  Let only a few volunteers practise aloud. Introduce new task demands during the readiness check. Rush to independent work to protect the planned schedule.
Check for impact
Most students succeed on a similar item without the teacher supplying each step.
The class can explain the process before release.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Guide Student Practice; StepFinder: Plan, Run and Monitor Independent Practice.

title: Purposeful independent practice
desc: Independent rehearsal and application of explicitly taught knowledge or skills, designed for accuracy, fluency and increasing automaticity.
text:
What it is: Independent rehearsal and application of explicitly taught knowledge or skills, designed for accuracy, fluency and increasing automaticity.
Why it helps: Repeated accurate retrieval and performance stabilise learning in long-term memory. Independence also gives the teacher cleaner evidence than heavily supported work.
Use it when: after students have demonstrated readiness through guided practice and a whole-class check.
Implementation sequence
Protect a planned point in the lesson for independent practice.
State the task, success criteria, expected working conditions and checkpoints.
Use tasks that mirror taught examples before adding complexity.
Let silence settle, then circulate early and systematically.
Correct error practice, adjust support and extend challenge gradually.
Revisit the knowledge later through spaced retrieval.
DO | DON'T
 Prioritise accuracy before speed. Set achievable sub-goals and visible checkpoints. Keep practice purposeful and connected to future performance. |  Use busy work unrelated to the learning goal. Release students before they are ready. Leave errors uncorrected until the end of the exercise.
Check for impact
Students sustain accurate work with decreasing prompts.
Fluency and later retrieval improve without sacrificing reasoning.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Purposeful Independent Practice and Independent Practice Checklist; StepFinder.

title: Scaffolding difficult tasks
desc: Temporary support such as a model, worked example, prompt, sentence stem, vocabulary bank, partial task or visual cue that preserves the ambitious task.
text:
What it is: Temporary support such as a model, worked example, prompt, sentence stem, vocabulary bank, partial task or visual cue that preserves the ambitious task.
Why it helps: A scaffold reduces an avoidable barrier or part of the load while keeping attention on the intended thinking. Its success is measured by the independence it enables.
Use it when: when the goal is appropriate but students cannot yet access a step because of prior knowledge, language, executive or processing demands.
Implementation sequence
Identify the exact barrier and the knowledge students already possess.
Choose the least support that gives a viable route into the task.
Explain how to use the scaffold and model it briefly.
Monitor whether it improves accuracy and thinking.
Reduce or remove support as soon as evidence permits.
DO | DON'T
 Plan the fade at the same time as the scaffold. Use different levels of support flexibly within the same goal. Ask students which support helped and why. |  Simplify the learning outcome or remove the hard thinking. Give every student the same permanent scaffold. Mistake task completion with a scaffold for independent mastery.
Check for impact
Students complete the same intellectual goal with less support over time.
The scaffold addresses the intended barrier rather than adding extra steps.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Provide Scaffolds for Difficult Tasks; BSCS Adaptive Teaching.

title: Fading support and backward fading
desc: Reducing a model or scaffold in small evidence-led steps, often removing the final step first while keeping the task and method stable.
text:
What it is: Reducing a model or scaffold in small evidence-led steps, often removing the final step first while keeping the task and method stable.
Why it helps: Large jumps from full model to blank page overload novices. Backward fading preserves the start of the process and transfers responsibility gradually until the full sequence is independent.
Use it when: multi-step procedures and extended responses after students have seen and understood a complete model.
Implementation sequence
Show a complete example and explain why each step matters.
Keep the model visible for the first guided attempt.
Remove the final step and ask students to complete it.
Remove additional steps gradually while keeping the task type stable.
Use checks to decide whether to fade, hold or temporarily restore support.
Confirm learning through a fully independent similar task.
DO | DON'T
 Fade based on competence rather than elapsed time. Ask students to justify visible and missing steps. Allow a progression to span multiple lessons. |  Remove the opening steps first and leave students unsure how to begin. Change the method and reduce support at the same time. Continue fading when widespread errors show students are not ready.
Check for impact
Accuracy remains stable as each support is removed.
Students can initiate and complete the process independently.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Fading Support; StepFinder: Use Backward Fading and Fade Scaffolds.

title: Circulation and actionable live feedback
desc: Purposeful movement through a planned route to scan, read, compare work with criteria and give brief feedback that prompts immediate improvement.
text:
What it is: Purposeful movement through a planned route to scan, read, compare work with criteria and give brief feedback that prompts immediate improvement.
Why it helps: Early systematic observation exposes misconceptions before they spread. Prompt-clue-direct feedback keeps students doing the cognitive work while allowing the teacher to support many pupils efficiently.
Use it when: guided and independent practice, especially where layout, method or written evidence can be scanned quickly.
Implementation sequence
Plan a route, success criteria, must-check students and likely errors.
Move systematically and use a brief scan-read-compare diagnostic.
Record exemplars, partial responses and misconceptions with quick notation.
Use prompt, then clue, then a precise direction only if needed.
Mark the exact location and bound the improvement task.
Return to check that the action was completed correctly.
DO | DON'T
 Break the plane early and maintain awareness of the whole room. Keep language economical and actionable. Use the evidence to decide whether feedback should become whole-class reteaching. |  Zig-zag only towards raised hands. Explain at length to one student while the rest become invisible. Give feedback without returning to close the loop.
Check for impact
All parts of the room and priority students are sampled.
Students make the requested improvement while the thinking is still live.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Circulation and Actionable Feedback; StepFinder: Circulate to Check for Understanding.

title: Practice for fluency, cumulative review and challenge
desc: Sequencing repeated, varied and spaced opportunities so accurate knowledge or processes become increasingly fluent and can be applied in more complex contexts.
text:
What it is: Sequencing repeated, varied and spaced opportunities so accurate knowledge or processes become increasingly fluent and can be applied in more complex contexts.
Why it helps: Fluency reduces the working-memory cost of component knowledge. Spacing and varied practice then strengthen retention and flexible use.
Use it when: knowledge and procedures students must retrieve or execute automatically as part of more complex performance.
Implementation sequence
Identify the component knowledge that should become fluent.
Begin with blocked or closely matched practice to establish the method.
Provide immediate correction and maintain productive success.
Increase quantity, spacing, variation and complexity gradually.
Mix in prior learning once students can discriminate which method applies.
Track performance across time, not only within one lesson.
DO | DON'T
 Use personal bests or carefully framed competition where motivating. Schedule cumulative retrieval after initial success. Retain explanation and reasoning alongside speed. |  Push speed before accuracy and understanding. Use random interleaving before students know the component methods. Repeat identical items so mechanically that students stop thinking.
Check for impact
Accuracy remains high as delay and variation increase.
Students select and execute the method with less working-memory demand.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder: Ensure Consolidation, Retrieval Quizzes and Increase the Challenge; DistilED: Retrieval and Independent Practice.

title: Precise individual feedback
desc: Brief information that identifies the exact gap and prompts the student to retrieve, correct, practise or improve while the work is still active.
text:
What it is: Brief information that identifies the exact gap and prompts the student to retrieve, correct, practise or improve while the work is still active.
Why it helps: Feedback is useful only when it changes subsequent thinking or performance. Prompting before telling preserves student cognition and helps diagnose whether the issue is knowledge or execution.
Use it when: during practice when an error is local to an individual or small group and can be corrected without interrupting the class.
Implementation sequence
Compare the work with the planned success criteria or model.
Locate the error and decide whether the student can self-correct.
Use a prompt, question or raised-error-awareness cue first.
Give a clue, model a small step or direct action only as necessary.
Require the student to correct and complete additional matched practice.
Return to verify the improvement.
DO | DON'T
 Praise the specific successful feature before addressing the gap where appropriate. Use precise verbs and point to the location of change. Turn recurring corrections into retrieval prompts. |  Give vague comments such as 'more detail' without an action. Complete the thinking or correction for the student. Assume verbal acknowledgement means the work improved.
Check for impact
The student makes an accurate correction and succeeds on a similar item.
The same error becomes less frequent in later independent work.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder: Give Individual Feedback; BSCS Feedback Principles.

title: Whole-class feedback and Show Call
desc: Reviewing a set of work to identify patterns, then teaching from common strengths, misconceptions and strategically selected examples rather than writing repeated individual comments.
text:
What it is: Reviewing a set of work to identify patterns, then teaching from common strengths, misconceptions and strategically selected examples rather than writing repeated individual comments.
Why it helps: Pattern-based feedback is efficient and can make quality visible to everyone. Its impact comes from modelling, comparison and student action, not from the feedback sheet itself.
Use it when: when several students share a misconception, success feature or next step, and when examples can improve collective understanding.
Implementation sequence
Review all or a representative set of work against the same criteria.
Record common strengths, misconceptions, exemplars and next actions.
Set a courteous, safe culture before displaying student work.
Make responses visible and compare, annotate or improve them live.
Require students to correct, redraft, rehearse or retry.
Re-teach and recheck where the error is widespread.
DO | DON'T
