 Select examples for their instructional value, not only because they are perfect. Use tick-with-me or annotation so students track the feedback actively. Highlight changed thinking and why it changed. |  Use whole-class feedback to avoid diagnosing individual work. Publicly expose a student or invite ridicule. Deliver a feedback monologue without improvement time.
Check for impact
Every student can identify and apply the relevant action to their own work.
A follow-up task shows improvement in the common gap.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Whole Class Feedback; StepFinder/TLAC: Show Call, Own and Track and Whole-Class Feedback.

title: Structured peer feedback
desc: Students use clear criteria and modelled language to identify a specific strength and an actionable improvement in a peer's work.
text:
What it is: Students use clear criteria and modelled language to identify a specific strength and an actionable improvement in a peer's work.
Why it helps: Giving feedback requires students to internalise quality and compare evidence with criteria. The receiver benefits only when suggestions are accurate, kind, specific and followed by action.
Use it when: after students understand the content and success criteria well enough to evaluate work reliably.
Implementation sequence
Model the feedback process using an anonymous or teacher-created example.
Provide a small number of precise success criteria and feedback stems.
Require observation and evidence before a suggestion.
Make feedback specific, referenced, actionable, prescriptive and kind.
Give the receiver time to clarify and improve the work.
Sample feedback quality as well as the resulting revision.
DO | DON'T
 Train students to distinguish praise from useful evidence. Use paired roles and a clear time limit. Check that feedback is technically accurate before action. |  Use peer feedback before students know what quality looks like. Ask for unrestricted 'two stars and a wish' comments. End after comments are exchanged without revision.
Check for impact
Feedback refers accurately to criteria and names a feasible action.
Revised work improves in the targeted feature.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Peer Feedback; StepFinder: Build a Culture of Feedback.

title: Feedback as detective work
desc: Diagnosing the underlying cause of a response before deciding what information, prompt, model or practice will move learning forward.
text:
What it is: Diagnosing the underlying cause of a response before deciding what information, prompt, model or practice will move learning forward.
Why it helps: The same visible error can arise from different causes. Treating feedback as diagnosis avoids generic correction and helps the teacher target knowledge, process, attention, fluency or self-regulation.
Use it when: when an error persists, appears across several students or does not respond to the first correction.
Implementation sequence
Define the intended performance and gather the student's current evidence.
Ask the student to explain the choice or process that produced the answer.
Classify the likely cause rather than merely naming the surface error.
Choose the smallest response matched to that cause.
Require correction and a similar transfer item.
Record a curriculum or teaching issue when the pattern is widespread.
DO | DON'T
 Use questions to reveal the student's model of the task. Distinguish missing knowledge from failure to apply known knowledge. Escalate from prompt to clue to model only as required. |  Correct the final answer without identifying the faulty step. Assume carelessness when knowledge may be insecure. Give the same feedback code to errors with different causes.
Check for impact
The selected response fixes the cause, not just the example.
The student succeeds on a related but non-identical task.
Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Feedback as Detective Work; StepFinder: Classify Student Errors.

title: Exit tickets and retrieval quizzes
desc: Brief independent end-of-lesson or cumulative questions designed for rapid analysis and a clear instructional follow-up.
text:
What it is: Brief independent end-of-lesson or cumulative questions designed for rapid analysis and a clear instructional follow-up.
Why it helps: Independent responses provide cleaner evidence than self-report and allow the next lesson to begin from actual gaps. Retrieval quizzes also consolidate and expose what requires further practice.
Use it when: when a small set of core knowledge or misconceptions should shape the next lesson or revision plan.
Implementation sequence
Choose a few questions focused tightly on essential learning.
Include likely misconceptions and formats that can be analysed quickly.
Set a threshold for success before administering the check.
Ensure independent completion without help or peer checking.
Divide responses by success, dig into the important gaps and decide the next action.
Link gaps to revision material and future retrieval.
DO | DON'T
 Sample deliberately if time prevents reviewing every response immediately. Prepare model answers and select one or two items for deeper feedback. Use the results visibly in the next lesson. |  Ask so many questions that analysis becomes unmanageable. Collect tickets without a planned response. Treat the ticket as a high-stakes grade rather than learning evidence.
Check for impact
The next lesson or homework directly responds to the diagnosed pattern.
Students can identify and retrieve the corrected knowledge later.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder: Use Exit Tickets and Retrieval Quizzes; BSCS Feedback and Homework Principles.

title: Close the feedback loop: Own and Track
desc: Ensuring students record the accurate answer, understand why it is accurate and visibly amend, annotate, redraft or re-practise their own work.
text:
What it is: Ensuring students record the accurate answer, understand why it is accurate and visibly amend, annotate, redraft or re-practise their own work.
Why it helps: Feedback that is heard but not acted upon rarely changes learning. Visible correction and a fresh attempt make the response accountable and allow the teacher to verify impact.
Use it when: after verbal, written, peer or whole-class feedback and after any reteaching episode.
Implementation sequence
State the exact action students must take and where it should appear.
Model the correction or success feature if needed.
Give protected time for every student to amend or retry.
Ask students to explain the change or the rule behind it.
Scan or sample the corrected work.
Use a related task later to test durable improvement.
DO | DON'T
 Make the action concrete, specific and visible. Get meta about both correct and incorrect answers. Praise changed thinking and successful self-correction. |  Move on after giving the answer without requiring a record. Accept a tick or copied model as proof of understanding. Reteach without rechecking.
Check for impact
Every student leaves with an accurate record and can explain the change.
The improved method transfers to a later task.
Sources informing this profile: StepFinder/TLAC: Own and Track; Tips for Teachers: Responsive Teaching.

title: Lesson Planning and Learning Episodes
desc: A learning episode is the time needed for pupils to grasp a novel idea. It does not have to fit neatly into one lesson: an episode may be shorter than a lesson or may span several lessons. Planning therefore st
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Lesson preparation. Secondary: Explain; Check and adapt; Secure learning through practice; Do Now.
Search terms | lesson planning; learning episode; prepare the learning; prerequisite; core question; hinge; memory; retrieval; interleaving; transfer
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: “Craig Barton Lesson Planning and learning episodes”.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
A learning episode is the time needed for pupils to grasp a novel idea. It does not have to fit neatly into one lesson: an episode may be shorter than a lesson or may span several lessons. Planning therefore starts with the learning, not the slide deck or activity sequence.
Prepare the learning, not the PowerPoint.
A practical planning sequence
1.  Define the key idea pupils should understand, not just the task they will complete.
2.  Identify the prerequisite knowledge needed to access that idea. This is where atomisation becomes especially useful.
3.  Plan the Core Questions or hinge points that will reveal whether pupils are ready to move on.
4.  Plan the instructional episode: Atomisation → I Do → We Do → Consolidation.
5.  Only then move to purposeful independent practice or problem-solving.
6.  Plan how the idea will be revisited later through future Do Nows, weekly mixed-topic low-stakes quizzes, mixed-topic homework, or deliberate interweaving with later content.
From initial security to transfer
The project summary captured a useful progression for planning practice beyond first success:
Secure: pupils can reproduce the new knowledge or procedure accurately.
Vary: change surface features while preserving the underlying idea.
Connect: link the idea to related knowledge and discriminate between similar cases.
Apply: use the learning in purposeful questions or contexts.
Transfer: use the idea in less familiar settings where the route is not immediately signposted.
Memory and retention
The learning episode is not complete simply because pupils were successful at the end of the lesson. The project summary explicitly linked planning to delayed retrieval: future Do Nows, mixed-topic low-stakes quizzes, mixed homework and interweaving previously taught content. This makes retention a planned feature of curriculum delivery rather than an afterthought.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Plan around key ideas and prerequisite knowledge. | Planning as a sequence of activities or slides without a clear learning endpoint.
Pre-plan the questions that will tell you whether pupils are ready to move on. | Assuming end-of-lesson performance means the idea is secure in long-term memory.
Treat the episode as flexible in length; let learning, not the bell, define its boundary. | Moving to independent practice because time has elapsed rather than because checks show readiness.
Schedule future retrieval while planning the episode. | Treating retrieval as a generic starter disconnected from curriculum scheduling.
Use all-student checks before independent practice. | 
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Lesson preparation: This is the strongest fit: define the endpoint, prerequisite knowledge, sequence, checks and future retrieval before the lesson.
Explain: The episode deliberately plans where I Do / explicit explanation is needed and how much new material is introduced at once.
Check and adapt: Core Questions and hinge points provide the evidence for deciding whether to move on, re-explain or extend.
Secure learning through practice: Practice follows sufficient modelling and guided practice, and progresses from security towards transfer.
Do Now: Future Do Nows are explicitly planned as delayed retrieval opportunities.

title: Atomisation
desc: Atomisation means breaking a routine, concept or performance down into the smallest teachable and assessable pieces needed for success. In the BSCS adaptation developed in the project, the key value is not the
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Lesson preparation. Secondary: Explain; Check and adapt.
Search terms | atomisation; atoms; prerequisite knowledge; representative example; endpoint; small steps; cognitive load; check prerequisites
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: “Craig Barton Atomisation summary”.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
Atomisation means breaking a routine, concept or performance down into the smallest teachable and assessable pieces needed for success. In the BSCS adaptation developed in the project, the key value is not the maths-specific taxonomy itself; it is the planning discipline of identifying what pupils must already know before the new explanation can work.
The BSCS planning routine: ATOMISE BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN
1.  Start with the endpoint: what will successful performance look like?
2.  Select a representative example or task that genuinely embodies the new learning.
3.  Atomise what pupils need to know or do to succeed on that example.
4.  Separate prerequisite atoms from genuinely new atoms.
5.  Plan how prerequisite atoms will be checked before the Explain phase.
6.  If the prerequisite check is insecure, fix the gap and re-check before layering on the new idea.
7.  Use the new atoms to decide the order and size of the explanation steps.
Decision rule from the project summary
Where prerequisite knowledge is not secure for a substantial proportion of the class, the response is not to press on with the planned explanation. The project summary used an approximate 80% security threshold: below that, explain or fix the prerequisite and then re-check.
Important distinction
Atoms are a teacher planning tool, not a list of lesson objectives to display to pupils. The purpose is to make expert knowledge structure visible to the teacher so that explanations and checks are more precise.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Choose a representative example first. | Turning every atom into a pupil-facing objective.
Separate prerequisite knowledge from new knowledge. | Importing an elaborate taxonomy when a simple prerequisite/new distinction is enough.
Check prerequisites before Explain. | Checking prerequisites after teaching the new content.
Use atoms to design smaller, coherent explanation steps. | Assuming a familiar-looking task means the underlying prerequisites are secure.
Re-check after a prerequisite fix. | 
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Lesson preparation: Directly strengthens anticipation of barriers, sequencing and planning the explanation.
Explain: Determines the smallest coherent steps and what can be treated as known versus what requires explicit teaching.
Check and adapt: Prerequisite checks generate actionable evidence before new content is introduced.

title: Do Now
desc: The Do Now is a consistent opening routine designed principally for spaced retrieval and a purposeful start. In the project summary, it is not primarily a prerequisite check for the new lesson; prerequisite che
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: 1: Do Now. Secondary: Climate and culture; Check and adapt; Lesson preparation.
Search terms | Do Now; retrieval; four questions; 3 of 4; 80%; timer; Book-to-Board; challenge; responsive review; spaced retrieval
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Do Now.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Purpose
The Do Now is a consistent opening routine designed principally for spaced retrieval and a purposeful start. In the project summary, it is not primarily a prerequisite check for the new lesson; prerequisite checking is a separate responsive-teaching decision point when needed.
Design
Use a consistent four-question structure, with an optional challenge question.
Aim for roughly three out of four correct on average: enough success to motivate, but enough difficulty to make retrieval worthwhile.
Order the questions from more accessible to more challenging where useful.
Prefer questions with a clear, single answer when the aim is rapid checking.
Keep the task short enough to protect lesson time: the project summary used roughly five minutes of work plus approximately five minutes of review as a useful benchmark.
Routine
1.  Have the task visible before pupils enter so no teacher explanation is needed to start.
2.  Use a visible timer and a silent, independent start.
3.  Complete two circulation laps where practical: one to secure the routine / register and one to gather information about learning.
4.  Latecomers join the task rather than interrupting the routine.
5.  If focus is poor, release one question at a time rather than abandoning the routine.
Checking and responsive review
The review should be proportionate to what pupils actually know. Book-to-Board MWBs, all-MWB responses, choral response, cold call or peer checking can be selected according to the question type. If almost everyone is correct, move quickly. If many are incorrect, model or re-teach the relevant point and then check again. Avoid giving hints before the check if those hints make the evidence unreliable.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Make the task immediately accessible and routine. | Using the Do Now as generic busywork.
Use spaced retrieval rather than only yesterday’s learning. | Turning every Do Now into prerequisite checking for today’s lesson.
Collect whole-class evidence efficiently. | Revealing clues that invalidate the retrieval check.
Review responsively rather than spending equal time on every question. | Lengthy whole-class review of items almost everyone has correct.
Engineer early success while preserving worthwhile difficulty. | Starting with teacher talk before pupils have begun.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Do Now: Direct enactment of the BSCS opening phase: immediate start, retrieval, early success and activation of prior learning.
Climate and culture: The predictable silent entry routine reduces transition time and secures purposeful behaviour.
Check and adapt: The review can generate evidence that leads to a quick model, targeted follow-up or re-teach.
Lesson preparation: Question selection should be deliberately spaced across the curriculum rather than improvised lesson by lesson.

title: Low-Stakes Quizzes for Memory and Retention
desc: The low-stakes quiz is a planned, substantial retrieval event designed to strengthen long-term memory. It is not simply a miniature test or a score-producing assessment. The project summary described a typical
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Do Now / long-term retrieval architecture. Secondary: Check and adapt; Lesson preparation.
Search terms | low-stakes quiz; LSQ; weekly quiz; mixed topic; 10 questions; confidence; worked solutions; review cards; retrieval; 80%
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: “Craig Barton low stakes quizzes”.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
The low-stakes quiz is a planned, substantial retrieval event designed to strengthen long-term memory. It is not simply a miniature test or a score-producing assessment. The project summary described a typical model of one weekly mixed-topic quiz of around ten questions, aiming for an average success rate of roughly 80%.
Routine
1.  Pupils retrieve answers independently and in silence.
2.  Before answers are revealed, pupils can record confidence in each response. This distinguishes a lucky correct answer from secure knowledge and, importantly, highlights high-confidence errors.
3.  Reveal complete worked solutions rather than only final answers.
4.  Prioritise review around high-confidence errors and important gaps.
5.  Create Review Cards or another personalised retrieval mechanism for the items that need revisiting.
6.  Schedule those items for future retrieval rather than treating correction as the endpoint.
Scores and stakes
The project summary generally advised against routinely recording quiz scores. The purpose is learning and memory: pupils should attend to what they know, what they misremember and what needs to be revisited, rather than optimising for a mark.
Why confidence matters
A high-confidence wrong answer is especially valuable diagnostic information because it points to knowledge that may be strongly encoded but incorrect. Those errors deserve priority in subsequent review and retrieval.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Mix material from different points in the curriculum. | Treating the quiz mainly as a score or grade.
Keep the quiz genuinely low stakes. | Only quizzing very recent content.
Use confidence ratings before answers are shown. | Showing answers before pupils have committed to a response.
Provide full worked solutions. | Assuming one correction has fixed a memory error.
Schedule future retrieval of errors through Review Cards or planned revisits. | Spending equal time on every item regardless of importance or confidence.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Do Now: The same retrieval principles can inform Do Now design, although the LSQ is a larger, less frequent retrieval event.
Lesson preparation: Memory and retention are deliberately scheduled across time rather than left to ad hoc revision.
Check and adapt: Confidence plus correctness reveals which knowledge needs re-teaching or planned retrieval.
Feedback to improve: Worked solutions and Review Cards convert quiz evidence into action rather than a mark.

title: Mini Whiteboards (Show Me Boards)
desc: Mini whiteboards maximise participation and give the teacher rapid, visible evidence from all pupils. Their value depends on a tight routine: everyone thinks, everyone commits, everyone reveals at the same mome
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Drive thinking for all; Check and adapt. Secondary: Do Now; We Do / guided practice.
Search terms | MWB; mini whiteboard; Show Me; boards up; whole-class response; scan; Book-to-Board; thinking time
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Mini Whiteboards.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
Mini whiteboards maximise participation and give the teacher rapid, visible evidence from all pupils. Their value depends on a tight routine: everyone thinks, everyone commits, everyone reveals at the same moment, and the teacher scans for patterns before deciding what to do next.
Core routine
1.  Ask a question that can be answered clearly on a board.
2.  Give genuine thinking time; the project summary used around 30 seconds where appropriate rather than rushing pupils to display.
3.  Pupils write while keeping boards private.
4.  Use a common reveal cue: “Boards up in 3, 2, 1.”
5.  Scan the whole class, prioritising patterns, misconceptions and indicator pupils rather than commenting on the first board you notice.
6.  Decide whether to move on, model, discuss, re-teach or ask a follow-up question.
Reliable data
The board routine should prevent copying and answer contamination. Standardised positioning and simultaneous reveal matter because the purpose is not merely participation; it is trustworthy evidence of individual thinking.
Useful applications from the project summaries
Book-to-Board checking during Do Now review.
Step-by-step We Do, where each procedural step is completed and checked before the next.
ABCD / diagnostic responses.
Follow-up re-checks after a teacher explanation.
Independent-practice interventions: “Show me how you got that.”
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Teach one consistent reveal routine. | Letting pupils hold boards up as soon as they finish.
Protect thinking time before boards go up. | Revealing or strongly cueing the answer before the scan.
Scan the class before revealing the correct answer. | Using MWBs for lengthy responses that are difficult to scan reliably.
Use what you see to adapt immediately. | Commentating on individual boards before you have read the class pattern.
Ask questions whose answers can be interpreted quickly. | Treating “boards used” as evidence that checking was effective.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Drive thinking for all: Every pupil must generate a response, raising participation and accountability.
Check and adapt: MWBs are the project’s preferred method for rapid whole-class evidence in many responsive-teaching moments.
Do Now: Book-to-Board and all-MWB routines can make review efficient and responsive.
Secure learning through practice: Step-by-step boards are a strong We Do structure before pupils work independently.

title: Checks for Listening
desc: A Check for Listening asks whether pupils attended to and can immediately reproduce what was just said or shown. It is different from a Check for Understanding, which asks pupils to apply, explain or transfer t
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Climate and culture + Explain. Secondary: Drive thinking for all; Check and adapt.
Search terms | checks for listening; active listening; attention; 100%; empty hands; Pastor’s Perch; Be Seen Looking; Explain Frame Reframe; silent teacher
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Checks for Listening / Explain phase.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Listening is not the same as understanding
A Check for Listening asks whether pupils attended to and can immediately reproduce what was just said or shown. It is different from a Check for Understanding, which asks pupils to apply, explain or transfer the idea. The distinction matters: during an I Do, the immediate instructional problem may be attention rather than understanding.
Conditions for listening
Empty hands and eyes on the teacher where appropriate.
Use a stable position for key instructions or explanations (the project summary referenced the “Pastor’s Perch”).
Be Seen Looking: visibly scan and wait for full attention.
Use a narrated countdown and least-invasive correction to secure 100% attention.
Step away from the board or visual when speaking so pupils know whether to look at the teacher or the representation.
Checking the listening
1.  Explain or demonstrate a short, carefully bounded idea.
2.  Pause and ask pupils to recall or repeat the key point: for example, “What was the question?”, “What did I say the first step was?” or a brief choral response.
3.  Use high-frequency cold call or call-and-response so listening is accountable for everyone.
4.  Where pupils missed the point, Explain → Frame → Reframe rather than simply repeating a longer version.
5.  Only then move to recording, rehearsal or a genuine Check for Understanding.
Silent Teacher
The Explain-phase summary also captured Barton’s “Silent Teacher” idea: explicitly announce a silent demonstration, insist on silence from pupils and use gesture, pointing and visible steps. Because the teacher is not talking, pupils attend closely to movement and often engage in low-stakes self-explanation and prediction. Pauses can be deliberately cued so pupils think about what comes next.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Plan listening checks into the explanation in advance. | Using “Any questions?” as evidence pupils listened.
Keep explanations short enough that pupils can reproduce the key idea. | Talking over novel text or while pupils are copying.
Use listening checks to maintain collective attention. | Asking a difficult application question when the immediate problem is attention.
Separate “Did you hear it?” from “Do you understand it?”. | Continuing an explanation while some pupils are visibly not attending.
Record or write only after the listening episode when copying would create split attention. | Making the listening check so elaborate that it destroys the flow of the explanation.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Climate and culture: Securing attention is a precondition for learning; the routine makes attention explicit and accountable.
Explain: Checks for Listening sit inside the I Do without turning the explanation into constant hybrid Q&A.
Drive thinking for all: Cold call and choral response keep all pupils mentally accountable during teacher explanation.
Check and adapt: Listening data tells the teacher whether to reframe the explanation before testing understanding.

title: Cold Call
desc: Cold Call means asking a question and then selecting a pupil regardless of whether their hand is raised. Used routinely, it raises the participation, thinking and listening ratio, gives the teacher a more repre
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Drive thinking for all. Secondary: Check and adapt; Explain; Turn and Talk follow-up.
Search terms | cold call; pause then name; representative sample; accountability; wait time; full sentence; technical vocabulary
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Cold Call.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
Cold Call means asking a question and then selecting a pupil regardless of whether their hand is raised. Used routinely, it raises the participation, thinking and listening ratio, gives the teacher a more representative sample of understanding, and makes mistakes feel less exceptional.
Routine
1.  Ask the question to the whole class first.
2.  Pause for thinking time.
3.  Then name the pupil: question → pause → name.
4.  Expect a complete response where the task demands it, including accurate disciplinary vocabulary.
5.  Use the answer to decide the next question or whether to broaden the sample.
Best uses
After Silent Solo or Everybody Writes.
After Turn and Talk, so the selected pupil has rehearsed an answer.
During explanation to check listening.
To sample understanding from different parts of the room rather than relying on the same volunteers.
To ask pupils to build on, compare or evaluate another answer.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Ask before naming. | Naming first, which lets everyone else stop thinking.
Use enough wait time that everyone has a real chance to think. | Using Cold Call mainly as a behaviour trap.
Use it frequently enough that it becomes normal. | Calling only on pupils likely to be correct.
Pair it with rehearsal when the response is demanding. | Assuming one cold-called answer represents the whole class.
Sample strategically across the class. | Removing wait time in the name of pace.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Drive thinking for all: Cold Call makes participation less dependent on volunteering and keeps everyone accountable.
Check and adapt: It can provide a quick sample, although whole-class methods such as MWBs are stronger when the decision requires reliable class-wide data.
Explain: Useful for checks for listening and brief recall without converting I Do into a long dialogue.
Turn and Talk: A strong sequence is Think / Write → Turn and Talk → Cold Call.

title: Call and Response
desc: Call and Response is a brief whole-class verbal response. It is efficient because it requires no equipment and can make everyone rehearse a key fact, term, phrase or routine. In the project summary, its value w
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Drive thinking for all. Secondary: Explain; Climate and culture; retrieval.
Search terms | call and response; choral response; EFR; vocabulary; oral rehearsal; whole-class response
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Call and Respond.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
Call and Response is a brief whole-class verbal response. It is efficient because it requires no equipment and can make everyone rehearse a key fact, term, phrase or routine. In the project summary, its value was greatest when the response was short, unambiguous and worth rehearsing.
Applications
Vocabulary pronunciation and definition stems.
Rapid retrieval of short facts or relationships.
Checks for listening during an explanation.
Knowledge-organiser self-quizzing and rehearsal.
Replacing unnecessary note-taking when the desired learning is accurate oral recall.
EFR and thinking time
For a response that requires thinking rather than simple repetition, use an Everybody-First-Respond / whole-class structure with at least a few seconds of thinking time. Choral response should not become an excuse to remove thinking.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Use for concise, common responses. | Using choral response for ambiguous or lengthy answers.
Model the exact quality of response expected. | Letting confident pupils shout first and cue everyone else.
Protect thinking time before a more demanding choral answer. | Mistaking a loud chorus for individual understanding.
Repeat until pronunciation or phrasing is precise where precision matters. | Using it as the only checking method for complex ideas.
Use it as one participation method within a wider sequence. | 
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Drive thinking for all: All pupils can rehearse a concise response simultaneously.
Explain: Supports checks for listening and vocabulary rehearsal without long interruptions.
Climate and culture: A predictable response routine can improve attention and collective participation.
Check and adapt: Useful as a listening check, but not sufficient by itself for diagnosing individual misconceptions.

title: Turn and Talk
desc: Turn and Talk is not simply “discuss with your partner”. The project summary treated it as a tightly structured thinking and rehearsal routine:
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Drive thinking for all. Secondary: Check and adapt; Explain; Secure learning through practice.
Search terms | Turn and Talk; partner talk; crest of the wave; think pair share; roles; listen; cold call; re-vote; 4-2
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Turn and Talk.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core routine
Turn and Talk is not simply “discuss with your partner”. The project summary treated it as a tightly structured thinking and rehearsal routine:
1.  Pose a question worth discussing.
2.  Give individual thinking time first (at least a few seconds; often with a jot or MWB response).
3.  Specify who speaks first using an unambiguous role.
4.  Partner A explains while Partner B listens.
5.  Switch so Partner B responds.
6.  End while discussion is still lively — at the “crest of the wave”.
7.  Harvest thinking through Cold Call, a re-vote, or a prompt that rewards listening rather than only speaking.
Make sure there is something to discuss
Turn and Talk is particularly productive when pupils have different answers, need to justify a method, or must compare reasoning. Useful prompts include: “Convince your partner”, “If you agree, explain why someone might disagree”, “Whose answer changed?”, or “What did your partner say that was interesting?”
Responsive-teaching uses
After a range of MWB / ABCD answers, especially when roughly 40–80% are correct.
After an all-hands-up or vote where the class is divided.
When no one initially volunteers: individual think → talk → Cold Call.
After an I Do to rehearse the explanation before We Do.
Inside 4–2 independent-practice cycles: four minutes silent work, two minutes paired discussion, then return to independent work.
Accountability
The pair should be accountable for the quality of talk and listening. The project notes stressed that “helping others is the hardest job”: praise and correction can be directed at pairs, and the final Cold Call can ask a pupil to report their partner’s thinking.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Give individual think time before talk. | “Talk to your partner” with no question or roles.
Assign the first speaker. | Using partner talk when everyone already has the same simple answer.
Use questions with genuine reasoning or comparison value. | Allowing one pupil to do all the thinking.
Stop at the crest of the wave rather than waiting for silence. | Ending the routine with no accountability.
Follow with a whole-class harvest or re-check. | Assuming talk itself proves the misconception has been resolved.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Drive thinking for all: Structures independent thinking, collaborative refinement and accountability.
Check and adapt: Useful when responses are mixed; discussion can be followed by a re-vote and teacher explanation.
Explain: Can provide rehearsal after an I Do without co-constructing the original explanation.
Secure learning through practice: The 4–2 cycle uses partner discussion to support sustained independent practice without turning the whole task collaborative.

title: Check for Understanding and Responsive Teaching
desc: Responsive teaching means changing what you do because of evidence about what pupils currently understand. A check is only useful if it can lead to a decision. The project summary therefore organised checking a
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Check and adapt. Secondary: Do Now; Explain; Secure learning through practice; Drive thinking for all.
Search terms | CFU; responsive teaching; 80%; 40-80%; under 40%; hinge; prerequisite; basics; independent practice; re-vote; What If
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: Craig Barton Responsive Teaching Framework / Check for Understanding.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core principle
Responsive teaching means changing what you do because of evidence about what pupils currently understand. A check is only useful if it can lead to a decision. The project summary therefore organised checking around specific decision points and response thresholds.
Five high-value CFU points in a lesson
1.  Do Now review.
2.  Prerequisite knowledge before teaching the new idea.
3.  The basics of the new idea after explanation.
4.  One or more hinge questions during the learning episode.
5.  Access to independent practice: are pupils ready to work successfully without the same level of support?
Gather reliable evidence
Avoid volunteers as the main source of data.
Cold Call gives a sample but can be incomplete or contaminated by prior answers.
ABCD can be efficient when the diagnostic question is well designed.
Circulation can be rich but takes time.
Mini whiteboards were the preferred whole-class method in the project summary for many decisions.
Do not reveal the answer before you have gathered the evidence.
Decision thresholds
Evidence | Interpretation | Response from project summary
≈80%+ correct | Nearly everyone is secure | Briefly reveal/model, keeping the final answer until the end; record the small number who need checking later; move on or use a “What if?” variation.
≈40–80% correct | Some are secure, some are not | Make responses visible; use warm call / Turn and Talk; re-vote; ask who switched and why; explain succinctly; ask a planned similar follow-up question.
<40% correct | Few are secure | Regain attention; re-explain or re-model in a different way; use Explain–Frame–Reframe and Checks for Listening; then ask a fresh follow-up CFU before continuing.
Worked example from the project summary
Do Now Q1: 28/30 correct → quick model, note the two pupils, move on.
Do Now Q2: 17/30 correct → display three different answers, Turn and Talk, re-vote, teacher explanation, then a planned similar follow-up question.
Explain after the check
When an explanation is needed, keep it concise enough that all pupils can explain it back. Focus on one thing at a time and use a concrete example. Pupils who were initially correct still need to attend: the teacher is building a shared, precise explanation, not only fixing the pupils who were wrong.
Revisit later
For the 40–80% and <40% pathways, the project summary also planned delayed checking through later retrieval, Do Nows, homework or a low-stakes quiz — sometimes one or two weeks later. Immediate success is not treated as proof of durable learning.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Choose checks because they inform a decision. | “Any questions?” as the main CFU.
Use all-pupil response methods where the decision is class-wide. | Moving on because a few volunteers are correct.
Keep the answer hidden until evidence is gathered. | Explaining for too long when only a tiny minority is insecure.
Pre-plan follow-up questions. | Repeating the same explanation unchanged when most pupils misunderstood.
Check again after explanation or adaptation. | Assuming successful re-teaching guarantees long-term retention.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Check and adapt: This is the direct operational model: gather evidence, interpret it, adapt, then re-check.
Do Now: The Do Now review is one of the five planned CFU points.
Explain: Prerequisite checks and post-explanation basics checks determine what to explain and whether to re-explain.
Secure learning through practice: The final checkpoint asks whether pupils have enough security to enter independent practice.
Drive thinking for all: Reliable CFU depends on high-participation response methods, especially MWBs.

title: Diagnostic Questions
desc: A diagnostic question is designed to provide a window into pupils’ thinking so that the teacher can make a better instructional decision. In practice, the project summary focused on multiple-choice questions wi
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Check and adapt. Secondary: Lesson preparation; Drive thinking for all; Explain.
Search terms | diagnostic question; multiple choice; distractor; misconception; ABCD; answer before options; explain wrong answers; make wrong answers correct
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project transcription/summary: Craig Barton Diagnostic Questions.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Definition and purpose
A diagnostic question is designed to provide a window into pupils’ thinking so that the teacher can make a better instructional decision. In practice, the project summary focused on multiple-choice questions with one correct answer and three distractors, where each distractor represents a plausible misconception or error.
What diagnostic questions can assess
Factual recall.
Procedural knowledge, including “who is correct?” comparisons.
Conceptual understanding, again often through comparing reasoning rather than only final answers.
Question-quality criteria
Distractors must be plausible and diagnostic, not silly.
There should be one unambiguously correct answer.
Prefer a single-step interpretation where possible.
Avoid grammatical cues, option-length clues and other test-wise shortcuts.
Design so pupils cannot arrive at the correct option for the wrong reason.
Five-step classroom routine
1.  Think in silence.
2.  Working out is allowed where appropriate.
3.  Rehearse an explanation for the chosen answer.
4.  No looking at other pupils’ responses.
5.  Show the answer on the common cue.
The project notes used roughly 5–10 seconds thinking time for many questions and recommended launching the routine with non-subject examples so pupils learn the mechanics before the diagnostic content matters.
Supercharging the question
Hide the answer options first and ask pupils to generate an answer before seeing the choices.
After identifying the correct option, ask why someone might choose each wrong answer.
Ask pupils to change a wrong option so that it becomes correct.
Use the response pattern to form temporary flexible groups while secure pupils complete deeper explanation or extension.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Write distractors from real misconceptions. | Using arbitrary wrong answers merely to fill four options.
Give thinking time before the reveal. | Showing options so early that recognition replaces retrieval when generation is possible.
Require pupils to commit simultaneously. | Revealing the correct answer before the whole-class vote.
Ask about the reasoning behind wrong answers. | Treating the percentage correct as the only useful information; the distractor pattern matters.
Use the response pattern to decide what happens next. | Using ambiguous multi-step wording that makes the diagnosis unclear.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Check and adapt: Each distractor should indicate a different likely misconception, making the next instructional move more precise.
Lesson preparation: Strong diagnostic questions are planned around anticipated errors; they are difficult to improvise well.
Drive thinking for all: Simultaneous ABCD / MWB responses make every pupil commit.
Explain: The diagnosis can determine exactly what must be re-explained and what can be left alone.

title: I Do: Explicit Explanation and Modelling
desc: The I Do is a teacher explanation or demonstration of new material, especially useful when novices are learning a new procedure or tightly structured way of thinking. The project summary emphasised that an I Do
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Explain. Secondary: Climate and culture; Lesson preparation; Check and adapt.
Search terms | I Do; worked example; explicit instruction; empty hands; visualiser; silent teacher; coherence; split attention; concise explanation
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project transcription/summary: Craig Barton Explain Phase / I Do.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
The I Do is a teacher explanation or demonstration of new material, especially useful when novices are learning a new procedure or tightly structured way of thinking. The project summary emphasised that an I Do is neither co-construction nor a long lecture nor a hybrid Q&A in which the teacher asks pupils to guess each next step.
Conditions for attention
Empty hands and eyes on the teacher during the core demonstration where copying would compete with attention.
Pupils copy or annotate immediately after the modelling rather than while the teacher is performing a novel step.
Use Checks for Listening inside the I Do; save genuine Checks for Understanding for the We Do / follow-up phase.
Announce and use Silent Teacher where a demonstration is more powerful without narration.
Designing the explanation
Plan and rehearse the explanation.
Keep it concise; the project notes highlighted very short, tightly planned explanations in mathematics as a useful discipline.
Break the idea into small coherent steps.
Use precise language and avoid vague transitions or “mazes”.
Use worked examples for novices.
Use a concrete example to anchor the explanation.
Choose examples, non-examples and representations deliberately.
Visual design and cognitive load
A visualiser is often preferable because pupils can see the hand, the developing representation and the sequence of decisions.
Step away when speaking so pupils know where to look.
Remove decorative or irrelevant visuals and words.
For diagrams, narrate the idea and then add labels rather than presenting everything at once.
Integrate text with the relevant part of a diagram; number steps where useful.
Do not talk over novel text that pupils are simultaneously expected to read.
Common sequence
The project learning-episode summary placed I Do inside a larger sequence: prerequisite check / atomisation → concise I Do → We Do → consolidation → purposeful independent practice or problem-solving → delayed retrieval.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Plan the explanation before the lesson. | Co-constructing every step with novices.
Use small steps and one main idea at a time. | A long uninterrupted lecture.
Keep pupils’ attention on the representation or demonstration. | Hybrid Q&A that slows the model and lets attention drift.
Use Checks for Listening to maintain accountability. | Pupils copying while they are supposed to watch a novel demonstration.
Move to We Do for genuine testing of the new learning. | Reading crowded slides aloud or talking over novel text.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Explain: Direct implementation of clear, explicit instruction, modelling, small steps, prior-knowledge links and cognitive-load management.
Lesson preparation: The quality of I Do depends heavily on planning the explanation, example, representation and likely sticking points.
Climate and culture: Empty-hands routines and Checks for Listening secure full attention.
Check and adapt: Prerequisites are checked before I Do; understanding of the new learning is checked afterwards rather than guessed during the model.

title: We Do: Guided Practice
desc: The We Do is the bridge between teacher modelling and independent practice. Pupils attempt the same underlying skill with support while the teacher gathers evidence about who is ready to work alone and who need
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Secure learning through practice. Secondary: Check and adapt; Drive thinking for all; Explain.
Search terms | We Do; guided practice; step-by-step MWB; Tick Trick; What If; Reset; Extension; worked example
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project transcription/summary: Craig Barton We Do.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Purpose
The We Do is the bridge between teacher modelling and independent practice. Pupils attempt the same underlying skill with support while the teacher gathers evidence about who is ready to work alone and who needs more guided practice.
Choose the question carefully
The We Do should require thinking without becoming a completely new problem. If it is almost identical to the I Do, pupils can copy a pattern without understanding. If it is too different, the teacher cannot tell whether the new learning itself is secure.
Board setup
The project summary recommended keeping the I Do visible on one side and revealing the We Do separately, allowing pupils to use the model without confusing the two examples.
Step-by-step MWB version
1.  Reveal the We Do only after the I Do is complete.
2.  Ask pupils to complete only the first step on their mini whiteboards.
3.  Scan the class.
4.  Write or confirm the correct step.
5.  Proceed to the next step only when the evidence justifies it.
Tick Trick → What If → Reset → Extension
Tick Trick: pupils compare their layout / working with a model and audit where marks or ticks are gained.
What If: change as little as possible in the question so pupils adapt their existing working rather than starting from scratch.
Reset: use a genuinely different question that requires a clean board and a fresh application of the method.
Extension: pose a question or variation pupils have not yet seen, moving beyond simple reproduction.
Recommended sequence from the project transcription
I Do → step-by-step We Do → Tick Trick → What If → Reset → Extension. The exact number of variations depends on the complexity of the procedure; the project notes cautioned against forcing multiple “What If” changes when the procedure is too large or the alterations would create excessive load.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Keep the I Do available as a model. | Jumping straight from I Do to long independent practice.
Use all-pupil response methods during guided practice. | Using an identical clone that rewards pattern copying.
Change enough to require thinking, but not so much that you are testing something else. | Making the We Do so novel that failure is uninterpretable.
Extend guided practice for pupils who are not yet secure. | Moving on because the most vocal pupils can do it.
Use small variations to reveal whether pupils understand the structure. | Using every variation type mechanically regardless of subject or task.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Secure learning through practice: This is the core guided-practice phase before responsibility is handed over.
Check and adapt: Every We Do response is data about readiness for independence.
Drive thinking for all: MWBs and step-by-step responses keep participation high.
Explain: The I Do remains visible and can be re-modelled if the check shows pupils are not ready.

title: Maximising Participation During Independent Practice
desc: Participation ratio is the proportion of pupils actively engaged in the learning task at a given moment. Two variables matter: how many pupils are participating and for how long. Independent practice is a commo
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Secure learning through practice. Secondary: Climate and culture; Drive thinking for all; Check and adapt.
Search terms | independent practice; participation ratio; Golden Silence; 30:30:30; active observation; Book-to-Board; 4-2; circulation; blackspots
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project transcription/summary: “Maximising the Participation Ratio During Independent Practice”.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Participation ratio
Participation ratio is the proportion of pupils actively engaged in the learning task at a given moment. Two variables matter: how many pupils are participating and for how long. Independent practice is a common point for the ratio to fall because pupils have more opportunity for a “cognitive break”. The aim is therefore sustained thinking, effort and accountability — not pupils merely looking busy.
Before practice begins
Secure silence and full attention before revealing or distributing materials that could distract from instructions.
Give clear, numbered instructions: what you are looking for, what you are not looking for, and what pupils should do when they finish.
Check that pupils listened. Display more complex instructions afterwards so they remain available during practice.
Use a clear release cue such as “Ready… [pause]… Go!”.
Where helpful, use an Instruction Sandwich or Repeated Instructions Game to strengthen the launch routine.
Protect the first 30 seconds: Golden Silence
The first moments establish the norm. The project summary recommended roughly 30 seconds of “Golden Silence”: thank pupils in advance, stand where the whole room is visible, Be Seen Looking, and correct unobtrusively. A least-invasive sequence can move from look → gesture → proximity → quiet word → anonymous reminder. Reset if the start collapses rather than accepting a weak norm.
Purposeful circulation and active observation
After Golden Silence, circulate with a route rather than wandering; eliminate classroom blackspots.
Check one thing at a time: effort, timing, a particular error or a presentation feature.
Visit strong pupils early as well as pupils likely to struggle; this helps establish the expected standard and prevents teacher attention being monopolised by need.
Use Book-to-Board circulation where a whole-class comparison will be useful.
Carry worked answers and, where useful, notes of anticipated misconceptions.
Take physical notes of patterns so you can decide whether to intervene individually or stop the class.
Step back from individual desks frequently to preserve whole-class visibility.
Individual intervention sequence
1.  Give specific praise for what is already successful.
2.  Give one precise next step or model.
3.  Check the pupil listened.
4.  Check they understand what to do next.
5.  Return later and re-check rather than assuming the intervention worked.
A useful MWB intervention from the project notes is: “Show me how you got that” → “Watch me model” → pupil retries → teacher returns later.
Whole-class interruption or leave them working?
Do not interrupt productive practice simply because the teacher has noticed something interesting. Stop the class when a common issue means continued practice would embed error, or when a brief Book-to-Board Quick Check will improve the work of many pupils. Otherwise preserve the uninterrupted practice time.
30:30:30 and 4–2 cycles
30:30:30: roughly 30 seconds silence to establish the start, 30 seconds circulating, 30 seconds standing back and observing the whole class before deciding the next move.
4–2 cycles: four minutes of silent independent practice followed by two minutes of paired discussion, then a return to independent work. The talk is a deliberate rehearsal / checking break, not permission for the whole practice phase to become collaborative.
Diagnostic review during practice
Short checks can be built into longer practice: a Critical Question, Book-to-Board Quick Check, or a prompt such as “Who got 8/10?” can identify whether a common error needs class-wide attention. The teacher’s response should be proportionate to the pattern, not automatic.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Frontload precise instructions. | Handing out distracting resources before instructions.
Protect the first 30 seconds. | Random circulation that leaves blackspots.
Circulate with a purpose and route. | Spending too long crouched beside one pupil and losing whole-class visibility.
Look for class patterns as well as individual errors. | Turning independent practice into constant teacher commentary.
Re-check pupils after individual intervention. | Assuming “quiet” means pupils are thinking.
Interrupt only when the learning gain justifies breaking practice. | Letting early finishers or stuck pupils create a drop in participation ratio.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Secure learning through practice: Directly strengthens purposeful independent practice, fluency and active observation.
Climate and culture: Golden Silence, Be Seen Looking and precise release routines create the conditions for sustained work.
Drive thinking for all: Participation ratio is the explicit success measure: number of pupils thinking × duration of thinking.
Check and adapt: Active observation, Critical Questions and class-wide interruptions are used to adapt practice from evidence.

title: Whole-Class Feedback
desc: The purpose of feedback is to change what pupils think or do, not to maximise the amount the teacher writes. The project summary therefore treated whole-class feedback as a diagnostic and instructional process:
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Feedback to improve. Secondary: Check and adapt; Secure learning through practice.
Search terms | whole-class feedback; WCF; barometer students; ticks and crosses; blank assessment; misconceptions; re-check; stretch; Review Cards
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: “Craig Barton Whole Class Feedback”.
Use this when | See the detailed guidance below; the strongest alignment is shown first.
Core idea
The purpose of feedback is to change what pupils think or do, not to maximise the amount the teacher writes. The project summary therefore treated whole-class feedback as a diagnostic and instructional process: identify class patterns, select the most important issues, teach them, re-check them and create personalised future retrieval where needed.
Diagnose patterns efficiently
Use ticks and crosses or another light-touch marking system to see patterns quickly.
Use barometer pupils if reading every script in detail would not change the class-wide diagnosis.
Annotate a blank copy of the assessment rather than writing repeated comments on every pupil’s paper.
Photograph or capture excellent examples and useful errors for modelling / Show Call.
Select around three widespread misconceptions for whole-class treatment. Isolated or careless errors may be better handled through retrieval opportunities rather than a long whole-class explanation.
Prepare the feedback lesson before returning work
The project summary emphasised giving the instructional feedback before returning the marked work, so attention stays on the model and the re-check rather than on individual scores and corrections.
Model → Re-check → Stretch
1.  Model the misconception or question type clearly.
2.  Ask an equivalent re-check question, ideally through mini whiteboards so everyone commits.
3.  Use approximately 80% as the threshold for whether the class is ready to move on.
4.  If secure, ask a harder stretch / variation question; if not, model again or change the explanation and re-check.
5.  Repeat this cycle for two or three high-value issues. The project summary suggested roughly 20 minutes as a useful scale for the main WCF sequence rather than trying to reteach an entire assessment.
Detective work and Review Cards
A strong end-point is a blank-copy “detective work” task in which pupils reconstruct a perfect version or identify how each item should have been approached. When work is finally returned, personalised Review Cards are more valuable than simply copying corrections: they turn individual errors into future retrieval targets.
Departmental routine captured in the project summary
Ticks/crosses + scores → identify three questions / issues → Model → MWB Re-check → Stretch → return work → Review Cards / future retrieval.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Select a small number of high-value class patterns. | Writing the same comment repeatedly on many scripts.
Prepare equivalent re-check questions in advance. | Returning work first and allowing scores to dominate attention.
Model before returning papers. | Explaining a misconception without a re-check.
Use whole-class responses to verify improvement. | Trying to reteach every error in one feedback lesson.
Turn individual errors into future retrieval targets. | Treating copied corrections as proof that the misconception is fixed.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Feedback to improve: Directly aligns: review patterns, address misconceptions, model improvement and ensure pupils act on feedback.
Check and adapt: The re-check determines whether to re-teach, move on or stretch.
Secure learning through practice: Equivalent questions provide immediate practice of the corrected idea rather than passive listening.
Drive thinking for all: MWB re-checks make the feedback episode accountable for everyone.

title: Walking-Talking Mock Exams
desc: Retain the valuable feature of a walking-talking mock - hearing an expert explain their thinking - but replace passive copying with a responsive cycle: pupils attempt, commit and rate confidence; the teacher di
text:
BSCS alignment | Primary: Check and adapt; Feedback to improve. Secondary: Secure learning through practice; Drive thinking for all; Lesson preparation.
Search terms | walking-talking mock; WTM; confidence score; 0-10; mini whiteboard; Step-by-Step; 80%; follow-up question; shadow paper; What If; Review Card; highest-confidence error
Project source | Prior T&L Strategies project summary: ‘Craig Barton Walking Talking Mocks’, based on Tips for Teachers: https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/walking-talking-mock-exams/
Use this when | Reviewing an exam paper or running a walking-talking mock where pupils need to think, reveal understanding, receive responsive modelling and leave with a quizzable revision resource.
Core idea
Retain the valuable feature of a walking-talking mock - hearing an expert explain their thinking - but replace passive copying with a responsive cycle: pupils attempt, commit and rate confidence; the teacher diagnoses; pupils receive only the explanation they need; understanding is checked again; secure pupils are stretched; and errors become future retrieval material.
Why the conventional version can fail
Pupils may copy without being cognitively active.
The teacher gathers no usable data, so every question receives similar time regardless of need.
Silence, nodding and neat notes create an illusion of understanding for teachers and pupils.
Pupils who are already secure gain little from repeated full explanations.
An annotated paper is difficult to use for practice testing and can default to rereading.
A responsive walking-talking mock sequence
1.  Attempt first. Work through one question at a time. Give slightly less than normal exam time so pace stays purposeful and every pupil attempts the question before seeing a model.
2.  Commit confidence. Before any answer is revealed, pupils record a 0-10 confidence score next to their response. This increases attention to feedback and identifies confidently held errors.
3.  Gather whole-class evidence. Pupils show the final answer on mini-whiteboards. For multi-step questions, ask for the first line of working using Step-by-Step. If boards are blank, ask pupils to identify the topic or first decision. In a hall, allocate staff a zone to scan.
4.  Respond proportionately. At roughly 80% or more correct, confirm or model briefly and preserve time for later questions. When understanding is less secure, boards down and hands empty: model the solution and narrate the thinking at each step.
5.  Re-check after explanation. Use a fresh follow-up question with the same context and comparable difficulty but enough variation to require thinking. Shadow-paper questions are useful. Re-check on mini-whiteboards. If pupils are still insecure, record the topic for fuller reteaching rather than pretending the mock alone has fixed it.
6.  Stretch secure pupils. Use a What If question that changes a condition, representation, required form or mark-scheme decision while preserving the underlying concept.
7.  Create Review Cards. Begin with each pupil's highest-confidence error. On the front, copy the question. On the back, record the topic, where to find further help or practice, the original mistake, a corrected worked example and annotations for the pupil's 'forgetful future self'. A practical target is three cards in ten minutes.
8.  Re-quiz later. Pupils answer the front of a card before checking the back. Correct cards move to the bottom of the deck; incorrect cards are studied and returned nearer the top so they recur sooner.
Do / avoid
Do | Avoid
Make pupils attempt one question before the explanation and record a 0-10 confidence score. | Teacher-led copying through every question before pupils have attempted it.
Use mini-whiteboards to reveal the final answer, first line of working or the topic when pupils are stuck. | Giving every question equal explanation time without first gathering evidence.
If understanding is insecure, model the thinking and then use a fresh, equivalent follow-up question. | Treating silence, nodding or neat copied solutions as evidence of understanding.
If understanding is secure, confirm efficiently and use a purposeful What If variation where it adds value. | Making already-secure pupils sit through lengthy explanations with no extension or variation.
Turn highest-confidence errors into Review Cards and schedule later self-quizzing. | Leaving pupils only with annotated papers that mainly invite rereading.
Explicit link to the BSCS model
Check and adapt: Mini-whiteboards and confidence scores reveal the class pattern; explanation time and the next question change in response.
Feedback to improve: The model, equivalent re-check and Review Card make feedback something pupils act on rather than merely receive.
Secure learning through practice: Pupils attempt before modelling, complete a fresh follow-up and then revisit errors through retrieval.
Drive thinking for all: Every pupil commits to an answer and confidence rating; staff scan all responses rather than relying on volunteers.
Lesson preparation: Select the questions, timing, diagnostic response, shadow/follow-up questions, What If variations and Review Card support references in advance.
Boundary: Barton's examples are rooted in mathematics. Preserve the active-attempt, diagnosis, re-check and revision principles when adapting to other subjects, but redesign the response format for the demands of that subject's exam questions.

title: Metacognition and self-regulation
desc: ALIASES: thinking aloud; plan-monitor-evaluate; self-questioning; metacognitive talk; gradual independence
text:
ALIASES: thinking aloud; plan-monitor-evaluate; self-questioning; metacognitive talk; gradual independence
BSCS COMPONENT: Lesson preparation; Drive thinking for all; Check and Adapt; Explain; Secure learning through practice; Feedback to improve
EEF EVIDENCE HEADLINE: +8 months average impact; very low cost; high evidence security; 355 studies; Toolkit review updated May 2025.
EVIDENCE STATUS: Direct EEF Toolkit evidence, supported by the EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance report, second edition (November 2025).
STUDENT PROBLEM: Students cannot explain their reasoning, select an approach, monitor progress, recover from error, transfer a method, or work independently without repeated teacher prompting.
MECHANISM: Pupils are explicitly taught how to plan, monitor and evaluate learning in a subject. Teachers model the hidden decisions of expert performance, prompt purposeful self-questioning and fade support as pupils become more independent.
KEY EEF FINDINGS
The Toolkit reports a high average impact, but also warns that the impact can be difficult to realise in ordinary practice.
Effective approaches explicitly teach strategies within normal curriculum content rather than as generic thinking-skills lessons.
Thinking aloud, worked examples, success criteria, reflection questions and structured reasoning can make expert processes visible.
Challenge needs to be sufficient for pupils to use a strategy, but not so great that the strategy cannot be applied successfully.
The 2025 guidance emphasises curriculum-embedded strategy instruction, scaffolding, metacognitive talk and planned movement towards independence.
DO
Model the cue, decision, monitoring check and correction - not just the visible steps.
Teach a small number of subject-specific plan-monitor-evaluate prompts and apply them to authentic tasks.
Use structured talk so pupils articulate why an approach works and how they know it is working.
Fade prompts, checklists and teacher narration once pupils show secure independent use.
Check whether pupils can select and use the strategy without being reminded.
DON'T
Teach generic 'learning to learn' activities detached from subject knowledge.
Label reflection as metacognition when pupils merely state whether they enjoyed or completed a task.
Overload pupils with long checklists or prompts that become another task to manage.
Assume that a teacher think-aloud is effective when it narrates actions but hides decisions.
Keep scaffolds in place after pupils can perform successfully without them.
AGENT USE: Recommend this when the learning problem concerns reasoning, transfer, self-correction or independence. Techniques such as thinking aloud and structured self-questioning are directly aligned. Do not attach the +8-month estimate to a single think-aloud routine.
Primary EEF sources: Toolkit: Metacognition and self-regulation; Guidance: Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning

title: Reading comprehension strategies
desc: ALIASES: activating schema; predicting; clarifying; inference; summarising; self-questioning; graphic organisers
text:
ALIASES: activating schema; predicting; clarifying; inference; summarising; self-questioning; graphic organisers
BSCS COMPONENT: Lesson preparation; Explain; Drive thinking for all; Check and Adapt; Secure learning through practice
EEF EVIDENCE HEADLINE: +7 months average impact; very low cost; moderate evidence security; 184 studies; Toolkit review updated October 2025.
EVIDENCE STATUS: Direct EEF Toolkit evidence. The BSCS link is strongest where pupils must understand subject texts, questions, source material or written explanations.
STUDENT PROBLEM: Students can decode words but do not understand a text, miss key information, struggle to infer or summarise, fail to connect text to prior knowledge, or cannot select a useful reading strategy.
MECHANISM: Expert reading processes are modelled and explicitly taught, then practised through guided and independent reading until pupils can select strategies for themselves.
KEY EEF FINDINGS
The Toolkit reports a high average impact across primary and secondary settings and across a range of subjects.
Successful approaches diagnose the barrier and match the text and strategy to pupils' reading capabilities.
Explicit modelling, guided practice and gradual release are important; a worksheet naming strategies is not sufficient.
Background knowledge and vocabulary strongly affect comprehension, especially for disadvantaged pupils and older struggling readers.
Pupils may struggle because of decoding, fluency, vocabulary, syntax, background knowledge or comprehension; the same response will not fit every cause.
DO
Identify the precise comprehension demand of the subject text or question.
Model how an expert reader notices cues, asks questions, clarifies and checks meaning.
Activate only the prior knowledge that is genuinely needed and pre-teach essential vocabulary.
Choose texts that are challenging enough to require the strategy but still accessible.
Move from explicit teaching to guided practice and then independent application across contexts.
DON'T
Assume every weak written response is caused by weak comprehension.
Use generic reading-strategy worksheets without modelling the thinking involved.
Ask pupils to predict or highlight without making the learning purpose clear.
Overload a short text with too many simultaneous comprehension prompts.
Keep pupils dependent on an organiser once they can comprehend independently.
AGENT USE: Recommend this for problems involving subject reading, command words, inference, extracting evidence or interpreting extended questions. Distinguish comprehension from decoding and vocabulary problems before selecting a technique.
Primary EEF sources: Toolkit: Reading comprehension strategies; Guidance: Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools

title: Feedback
desc: ALIASES: live feedback; whole-class feedback; verbal feedback; written feedback; self-correction; redrafting; Show Call
text:
ALIASES: live feedback; whole-class feedback; verbal feedback; written feedback; self-correction; redrafting; Show Call
BSCS COMPONENT: Check and Adapt; Secure learning through practice; Feedback to improve; Lesson preparation
EEF EVIDENCE HEADLINE: +6 months average impact; very low cost; high evidence security; 155 studies; Toolkit review updated June 2021.
EVIDENCE STATUS: Direct EEF Toolkit evidence, supported by Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning (2021) and the 2026 Check. Adapt. practitioner tool.
STUDENT PROBLEM: Students repeat errors, cannot see the gap between current and successful performance, ignore comments, do not improve work, or wait passively for teacher correction.
MECHANISM: Information about current performance redirects either teacher or pupil action towards a clear learning goal. Impact depends on strong initial teaching, evidence of the learning gap, appropriately timed information and pupils actually using it.
KEY EEF FINDINGS
Feedback is well evidenced, but not all feedback improves learning and poorly designed feedback can have negative effects.
Task, subject and self-regulation feedback tends to be more useful than comments about personal traits.
The principles matter more than whether feedback is written, verbal, digital, individual or whole class.
EEF guidance places high-quality instruction and formative assessment before the feedback itself.
Teachers should plan how pupils will receive and use feedback; comments without pupil action do not close the loop.
DO
Anchor feedback to a clear learning intention, model or success criterion.
Identify the most important gap and give information that enables a feasible next action.
Choose timing and method according to the task, pupil and learning need.
Protect time for correction, redrafting, rehearsal or fresh practice.
Use whole-class or live feedback when it is more proportionate and instructionally useful than extensive marking.
DON'T
Confuse the quantity of marking with the quality of feedback.
Give vague praise, grades alone or comments focused on personal characteristics.
Provide so many targets that attention is dispersed and action becomes unlikely.
Use feedback to compensate for unclear explanation, weak modelling or a poorly designed task.
Specify one universal feedback method or frequency regardless of context.
AGENT USE: For Show Call, whole-class feedback or live feedback, describe the technique as a delivery method aligned with EEF feedback principles. Do not claim that the EEF independently assigns +6 months to that named classroom routine.
Primary EEF sources: Toolkit: Feedback; Guidance: Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning; EEF: Check. Adapt.

title: Oral language interventions
desc: ALIASES: dialogic teaching; structured classroom talk; vocabulary talk; speaking and listening; purposeful questioning
text:
ALIASES: dialogic teaching; structured classroom talk; vocabulary talk; speaking and listening; purposeful questioning
BSCS COMPONENT: Drive thinking for all; Explain; Check and Adapt; Climate and culture
EEF EVIDENCE HEADLINE: +6 months average impact; very low cost; high evidence security; 188 studies; Toolkit review updated May 2025.
EVIDENCE STATUS: Direct EEF Toolkit evidence for oral-language approaches. The evidence base is strongest for literacy and reading-comprehension outcomes.
STUDENT PROBLEM: Students give short or imprecise explanations, do not use subject vocabulary, cannot articulate connections, participate unevenly in discussion, or fail to listen and respond to others' ideas.
MECHANISM: Purposeful spoken interaction supports vocabulary, explanation, connection-making and metacognitive awareness. Adults model and scaffold high-quality speaking and listening while talk is integrated with curriculum content.
KEY EEF FINDINGS
The EEF reports a high average impact, with the strongest evidence for approaches integrated into the curriculum.
Interaction between teacher and pupils and between peers is a central feature.
Vocabulary teaching is stronger when words are connected to current curriculum content and used actively and meaningfully.
Evidence is mainly based on literacy and reading-comprehension outcomes; the impact on science and mathematics attainment is less clear.
Professional development and deliberate design are important; merely increasing the amount of talk is not the intervention.
DO
Set a precise question, thinking time, speaking structure and intended product.
Model the language, reasoning and listening behaviours pupils are expected to use.
Require active use of essential subject vocabulary in meaningful explanations.
Structure accountability so every pupil thinks, speaks, listens and can report the pair's idea.
Follow discussion with an independent check when individual understanding matters.
DON'T
Treat any pupil conversation as evidence-informed oral-language practice.
Use open-ended pair talk without thinking time, roles, time limits or an outcome.
Allow confident pupils to dominate while quieter or lower-prior-attaining pupils remain passive.
Assume verbal fluency is the same as secure subject understanding.
Generalise the +6-month literacy-dominated estimate to a single Turn and Talk in any subject.
AGENT USE: Use this as the strongest EEF evidence link for well-structured Turn and Talk, vocabulary rehearsal and dialogic questioning. Cold Call can help sample subsequent understanding but is not itself evaluated by this Toolkit strand.
Primary EEF sources: Toolkit: Oral language interventions; Guidance: Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools

title: Peer tutoring
desc: ALIASES: reciprocal tutoring; peer explanation; trained peer support; structured peer assessment
text:
ALIASES: reciprocal tutoring; peer explanation; trained peer support; structured peer assessment
BSCS COMPONENT: Drive thinking for all; Secure learning through practice; Feedback to improve
EEF EVIDENCE HEADLINE: +6 months average impact; very low cost; high evidence security; 145 studies; Toolkit review updated May 2025.
EVIDENCE STATUS: Direct EEF Toolkit evidence for structured peer tutoring, not for every occasion when pupils help or assess one another.
STUDENT PROBLEM: Students need additional consolidation, explanation or feedback; some pupils benefit from rehearsing knowledge by teaching it; peer assessment is superficial or inaccurate.
MECHANISM: Learners take defined responsibility for explicit teaching support and evaluation. Both tutor and tutee can benefit when roles, materials and feedback processes are trained and monitored.
KEY EEF FINDINGS
Peer tutoring tends to be strongest for reviewing or consolidating taught material rather than introducing new content.
Training for staff and pupil tutors is essential, as are structure and time to improve the approach.
Low-attaining pupils may benefit particularly in the tutee role, but fixed roles can create dependency or low expectations if poorly designed.
The evidence concerns planned tutoring approaches, often delivered in intensive blocks, rather than a brief instruction to compare answers.
DO
