Change as little as necessary. A small consequential alteration makes the relationship easier to inspect.
Ask for a prediction first. Students can state what they expect to change and what will remain true.
Use Tick Trick thoughtfully. Compare working with the model to identify the decisions or criteria that earn credit.
Reset when needed. A clean, distinct example tests whether students can start the method independently.
Extend after security. A demanding variation is more useful when the basic method is sufficiently understood.
Preserve the underlying concept.
Ask for the reason the answer changes.
Changing several unfamiliar demands simultaneously.
Using extension while the original decision remains insecure.

title: PR09 · Golden Silence and active observation: launching independent practice
desc: Use Golden Silence and active observation to protect the launch of independent practice. Establish the working norm, then alternate purposeful circulation with a view of the whole class.
text:
Use Golden Silence and active observation to protect the launch of independent practice. Establish the working norm, then alternate purposeful circulation with a view of the whole class.
Prepare the launch. Give clear instructions, a stuck protocol and a useful finish task, then check listening before release.
Protect Golden Silence. Use a brief period of visible whole-class observation to establish independent effort.
Circulate purposefully. Inspect a specific feature of early work along a planned route and give short targeted feedback.
Step back and decide. Regain a view of the room, identify participation gaps and distinguish individual need from a common error.
Continue or reset. Preserve productive practice, use a brief class repair when justified, or a planned discussion break followed by renewed independent work.
“Begin independently. I will watch the first thirty seconds, then check first attempts. If you need help, identify the step that is unclear while continuing what you can.”
After checking instructions, the teacher protects a brief silent launch from a position with a whole-room view. Circulation then checks first attempts along a route, followed by a step back to inspect participation. A targeted prompt is revisited later. The teacher avoids spending the opening minutes absorbed at one desk.
Protect roughly the first thirty seconds. Stand where you can see the room, recognise the expected start and correct unobtrusively.
Use 30:30:30 flexibly. A brief launch, circulation period and step-back observation can stop individual support absorbing all attention.
Eliminate blackspots. A planned route should reach every part of the room, not just raised hands.
Give one precise intervention. Prompt the next step, check it was heard and return after the student works.
Use 4–2 cycles selectively. A short independent burst followed by paired checking can sustain thinking when it serves the task; it is not a compulsory timer routine.
Secure the start before extended individual help.
Step back regularly to observe the whole room.
Circulating into a long conversation immediately.
Treating silent appearance as evidence that everyone is thinking.

title: CA11 · Confidence scores: finding confidently held errors
desc: Use confidence scores alongside answers to identify uncertainty and confidently held errors. Confidence adds context to performance; it does not replace evidence of knowledge.
text:
Use confidence scores alongside answers to identify uncertainty and confidently held errors. Confidence adds context to performance; it does not replace evidence of knowledge.
Choose the use. Apply ratings to selected quiz or assessment answers where the information can guide feedback.
Explain the scale. Use clear endpoints and establish that honest uncertainty is helpful.
Attempt and rate. Students answer independently and record confidence before solutions or discussion.
Compare with accuracy. Identify confident errors, uncertain correct answers and insecure knowledge, then probe where needed.
Plan the response. Give relevant feedback and future practice, using high-confidence errors for Review Cards where appropriate.
“Before we reveal the solution, rate how confident you are that your answer is correct. We will compare confidence with the evidence and choose what to revisit.”
A quiz answer is wrong despite a high confidence rating. The teacher uses that mismatch to prioritise the explanation and a Review Card. A correct but uncertain answer receives a reasoning check and further practice. Ratings provide useful context to observed performance, rather than a separate attainment measure.
Commit before feedback. Ratings made after seeing the answer cannot reveal the original certainty.
Use a simple scale consistently. For example, explain what the ends of a 0–10 scale mean without turning every number into a complex rubric.
Prioritise confident errors. They are useful candidates for explanation, comparison and Review Cards.
Investigate low-confidence correct answers. The student may need fluency practice or may have guessed.
Keep the tone neutral. Honest uncertainty is more useful than students inflating ratings to appear successful.
Record a rating beside an independent answer.
Use the mismatch to guide review.
Treating confidence as attainment.
Rating only after the correct answer is public.

title: CA12 · Learner-generated examples: testing concept boundaries
desc: Use learner-generated examples to test the boundaries of a concept. Constraints help students move beyond the first obvious example and expose what they think counts.
text:
Use learner-generated examples to test the boundaries of a concept. Constraints help students move beyond the first obvious example and expose what they think counts.
Choose the concept. Identify the defining feature students should apply and confirm they have encountered it.
Generate a first example. Give silent time and collect a bounded response before sharing suggestions.
Broaden the range. Ask for another valid example, then an unusual example or one satisfying an added constraint.
Test the boundary. Ask for a convincing non-example and an explanation of the feature that excludes it.
Compare and refine. Discuss selected cases, correct the definition where necessary and test a fresh constraint individually.
“Give one example, another example and one that no one else is likely to choose. Finally, give a non-example that could fool someone, and explain the difference.”
In Languages, students generate a valid sentence, a second valid example and one satisfying an added constraint. They then write a plausible incorrect example and explain the rule it breaks. The range reveals whether pupils understand the grammatical boundary or rely only on the first familiar sentence pattern.
Ask for several examples. A second or unusual example reveals more than a single familiar case.
Add purposeful constraints. Specify a feature that forces students to reconsider the concept rather than repeat their first answer.
Include a plausible non-example. Ask for a case someone might think valid and explain why it is not.
Inspect boundary reasoning. Students should justify membership using the definition rather than how unusual the example looks.
Teach the concept first. Generating examples is most useful when students have enough knowledge to test the constraints.
Use constraints that expose the defining feature.
Require explanations as well as examples.
Unbounded example generation with no criterion.
Treating unusual answers as automatically sophisticated.

title: PR10 · Consolidation: securing new learning before independent practice
desc: Use consolidation after initial explanation and guided practice to secure the new idea before increasing independence or complexity. Make students reconstruct and explain the learning.
text:
Use consolidation after initial explanation and guided practice to secure the new idea before increasing independence or complexity. Make students reconstruct and explain the learning.
Select the central learning. Identify the principle or process students should retain from the episode.
Ask for reconstruction. Use a brief explanation, completion task or related attempt that requires students to recall and organise the idea.
Compare thoughtfully. Let students inspect a model or another response and explain meaningful differences.
Repair the insecure component. Re-model a specific gap and give another fresh attempt where necessary.
Connect the next stage. Move into purposeful independent practice or application when sufficiently secure, and plan a later retrieval return.
“Without looking at the model, explain the first decision and complete a related example. Then compare your method and identify the step you need to practise.”
After guided practice, pupils reconstruct the key method and complete a short related task with less visible support. Comparison with the model reveals one insecure decision, which gets a focused repair. A later retrieval return is planned. Consolidation secures the episode without being treated as proof that the learning will remain accessible permanently.
Keep it focused on the new learning. A broad topic recap may miss the specific decision taught in this episode.
Require an active response. Explanation, completion or a short independent attempt shows more than rereading the model.
Use the model deliberately. Let students compare initially, then remove it for a fresh attempt.
Do not equate consolidation with easy work. Students should think about the key relationship, not merely copy a summary.
Connect to later retrieval. Consolidation helps initial security; spaced returns are still needed.
Reconstruct the important idea or process.
Use the response to decide readiness.
A final slide that students passively reread.
Assuming immediate success removes the need for later retrieval.

title: PR11 · Problem-solving: applying secure knowledge in less familiar tasks
desc: Use problem-solving to help students apply secure knowledge when the route is less familiar. Plan the extra decision demand rather than disguise new teaching inside a complex task.
text:
Use problem-solving to help students apply secure knowledge when the route is less familiar. Plan the extra decision demand rather than disguise new teaching inside a complex task.
Identify the transferable knowledge. Confirm students can use the relevant concepts and procedures in familiar tasks.
Select the new demand. Change the context, representation or route choice while keeping the underlying content accessible.
Plan and represent. Students identify known information, the goal and a useful diagram or structure.
Attempt with purposeful support. Use prompts, comparison or modelling when the search reveals a specific barrier.
Compare and generalise. Discuss approaches and the clues that selected them, then apply the reasoning to another task.
“What do we know, what are we trying to find and which relationship could connect them? Sketch the situation before selecting your approach.”
In Maths, pupils use familiar methods in a task where the approach is not labelled. They represent the problem, identify useful information and justify the selected route. When a barrier concerns a taught relationship, the teacher prompts or models that point. A final comparison explains why alternative routes do or do not work.
Check the knowledge base first. Students cannot reason effectively with relationships or methods they have not learned.
Separate selection from execution. Ask which approach fits and why before completing every step.
Teach a useful heuristic explicitly. A diagram, simpler case or organised list can support the task without becoming a universal trick.
Model when search becomes unproductive. Sustained confusion may need guidance rather than more unguided time.
Compare routes after solving. Explain why different approaches work and when each is useful.
Match the unfamiliar demand to secure knowledge.
Discuss the reasoning behind the chosen route.
Calling an untaught procedure problem-solving.
Valuing struggle without attending to whether it produces learning.

title: LP07 · Purpose: helping students understand what they are learning and why
desc: Use a clear purpose to help students understand what the lesson is building towards and why the learning matters. Connect activities to the knowledge, performance or later use.
text:
Use a clear purpose to help students understand what the lesson is building towards and why the learning matters. Connect activities to the knowledge, performance or later use.
Define the destination. State the knowledge or performance students will develop, using language they can understand.
Select a concrete frame. Use an endpoint question, model or meaningful application to show what the learning enables.
Connect the first step. Explain how today’s component contributes to the larger idea.
Keep the purpose visible in practice. Refer to it when choosing examples, checking a decision or explaining an improvement.
Return to the destination. Ask students to use the learning in the original question or a related task so the purpose has a concrete outcome.
“We are learning how evidence supports a historical judgement. This paragraph gives us a way to compare explanations rather than list events.”
A Product Design lesson frames material properties through a concrete selection problem. The teacher explains how each taught property helps justify the choice. Practice returns to that same decision with a different product. The purpose connects activity to disciplinary reasoning rather than an artificial claim that every detail has an immediate everyday use.
Name the learning rather than the activity. “Explain the cause” is clearer than “Complete the worksheet.”
Keep purpose concrete. A question, performance or problem can make the destination visible.
Show a genuine connection. Use the curriculum or subject application rather than an invented claim that every idea is needed in daily life.
Revisit at the decision point. Explain how the current step contributes to the endpoint.
Preserve curiosity without delaying instruction. A hook is useful when it directs attention towards the learning, not when it becomes a separate entertainment.
Connect the task to a clear learning destination.
Use a meaningful subject rationale.
An activity label presented as the purpose.
A lengthy motivational introduction unrelated to the content.

title: DN06 · Retrieval homework: revisiting learning beyond the lesson
desc: Use retrieval homework to revisit taught knowledge between lessons. Make the independent attempt possible, provide useful feedback and connect gaps to future teaching.
text:
Use retrieval homework to revisit taught knowledge between lessons. Make the independent attempt possible, provide useful feedback and connect gaps to future teaching.
Select the retrieval content. Choose important taught knowledge and procedures, including planned returns to older topics.
Keep the task manageable. State the response, approximate scope and how students should act when stuck.
Protect the attempt. Give instructions to work independently before checking solutions or a support reference.
Build corrective feedback. Provide accurate explanations or worked solutions and a way to record consequential errors.
Connect to the next lesson. Recheck selected items, address common gaps and schedule further retrieval where needed.
“Try these questions from memory first. Then use the worked solutions to identify errors. Bring one question you need to revisit; we will check the main decisions next lesson.”
A Science homework mixes taught calculations and older retrieval. Pupils attempt before checking worked solutions and record one error to revisit. The next lesson uses a pivotal related question to sample the learning. The homework supports retrieval and feedback rather than becoming independent discovery of a procedure students have never been taught.
Use taught, accessible content. Homework should not rely on students discovering a new method without instruction.
Separate attempt and solution. Students need a chance to retrieve before checking worked answers.
Mix recent and older learning. A deliberate sequence strengthens return to important knowledge across time.
Provide a help route. A specific model, resource or reference supports students when recall fails.
Use the result in class. Sample a pivotal item or misconception so homework informs later retrieval and explanation.
Set homework through the current BSCS arrangements.
Use feedback and later retrieval.
Untaught independent content as retrieval.
Checking completion without attending to the learning.

title: DN07 · Getting students on board with retrieval: explain, demonstrate and build habits
desc: Use an explanation and demonstration of retrieval when students see quizzes as judgement or prefer familiar rereading. Help them understand why attempting recall is part of learning.
text:
Use an explanation and demonstration of retrieval when students see quizzes as judgement or prefer familiar rereading. Help them understand why attempting recall is part of learning.
Identify the concern. Find out whether students fear scores, do not understand the purpose or lack a useful retrieval routine.
Explain simply. Describe how trying to recall differs from rereading and why feedback follows the attempt.
Demonstrate with accessible content. Let students experience independent recall and checking without making the task a test of self-worth.
Establish the routine. Use predictable instructions, achievable demands and respectful responses to errors.
Reinforce the learning purpose. Show how previous gaps return in future practice and how students can use retrieval independently.
“You may recognise this when reading it, but can you produce it without the page? Try first; the gap tells us what to practise, and the feedback helps repair it.”
A teacher explains why recognising a paragraph is different from producing its key idea without looking. Pupils try an accessible recall task, receive feedback and meet the same knowledge again later. The routine demonstrates a learning purpose and treats errors respectfully, helping build trust in retrieval beyond a single explanation.
Explain the learning purpose. A low-stakes attempt strengthens access to knowledge and shows what to revisit.
Demonstrate a fair comparison. Use a simple experience to contrast recognition with generating an answer, without promising an instant universal result.
Normalise effort. Difficulty recalling is information about the learning, not a reason to avoid the attempt.
Make success attainable. Use well-taught content and a useful prompt where total failure would prevent productive practice.
Keep the routine consistent. Repeated experiences of attempt, feedback and improvement build more trust than a single motivational speech.
Explain the purpose and give corrective feedback.
Use mistakes to guide future practice.
A public ranking that undermines the low-stakes message.
Claiming effortful failure is always beneficial.

title: DT12 · Precise answers / Don’t round up: helping students refine a response
desc: Use precise-answer routines when a partly correct response is being accepted as complete. Help the student improve the answer rather than silently replacing it with your own explanation.
text:
Use precise-answer routines when a partly correct response is being accepted as complete. Help the student improve the answer rather than silently replacing it with your own explanation.
Listen to the actual answer. Judge what the student said against the intended knowledge rather than what you think they meant.
Name the useful start. Recognise the accurate element and identify the missing or imprecise feature.
Prompt a revision. Use a clue, key term, criterion or short rehearsal to make improvement achievable.
Return for the full answer. Ask the pupil to articulate the complete explanation, then involve listeners in restating or applying it.
Check a fresh case. Use a related question when needed to establish that the refined reasoning can be used beyond the rehearsed wording.
“You have the main idea. Say it again using ‘concentration’ and explain which way the particles move. I will give you a moment to prepare.”
A pupil’s answer contains a correct idea but omits the condition that makes it valid. The teacher recognises the accurate start, prompts the missing feature and returns to the pupil for the full explanation. A new example follows. The teacher does not silently supply the condition and treat the original response as complete.
Identify the missing feature. Decide whether the issue is vocabulary, evidence, a condition or the relationship between ideas.
